utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. We will now start the second day of our hearings of the merits of the appeal of Mr. Krstic, and we will start from a -- from the Defence, who will continue with their submissions. The counsel for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Just very briefly, after I finish my argument, Your Honours, my colleague, Mr. Petrusic, is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: -- on and how General Krstic never ordered troops from the Bratunac Brigade to assist in those executions or the later executions at Pilica Dom. Mr. Petrusic will also speak briefly to the issue of sentencing. I hope I learned my lesson yesterday about the rapidity of my speech, and I will really make quite an effort this morning not to overburden the interpreters. Just very briefly by way of recapitulation, we were talking about the Commission of Experts' report, the report that said that destroying the social fabric of the community by killing the elite, the leaders, and the military personnel, coupled with other heinous crimes such as deportation, can constitute genocide. That was in the report of the Commission of Experts. That was adopted precisely by the Trial Chamber in this case. Our claim is that the report of the Commission of Experts, both in terms of providing for qualitative genocide and also in terms of providing genocide for deportation, is an error, and we tried to show that by, we hope, a close analysis of the genocide statute and its drafting history. I now want to talk about the Commission of Experts, this organisation that had so much impact on the opinion, because we want to show in essence that it was a fact-gathering body, that it was not a body meant to enunciate lasting principles of law for a court to follow. And yesterday I was speaking about the -- the formation of the group, the chairmanship of Professor Fritz Kalshoven, and then following his resignation the chairmanship of Sherif Bassiouni. And the commission commenced its activities in November 1992 and concluded its work in April 1994. The commission furnished two interim reports to the Secretary-General, providing a record of grave breaches of the Geneva Convention and other violations of international humanitarian law. It was on the basis of one of these interim reports of the Commission of Experts that the Secretary-General noted that violations of international law had been committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and that view of this, the establishment of an international tribunal was suggested to bring justice to those persons responsible. The final report of the commission included a survey of the Commission's work since its inception, its substantive findings of alleged crimes of ethnic cleansing, genocide, and other violations, and its views on selected legal issues of particular significance in this factual context. In short, the Commission of Experts did indeed render valuable service to the Secretary-General and the Security Council in its mission of gathering evidence to bring perpetrators of crimes to justice. Our criticism of the Commission of Experts has to do only with its various legal findings and comments which -- which form a very small part of this 82-page report, which we have reprinted in full in our Annex 3. However, I think it's fair to say that the Commission of Experts never intended that its comments on legal issues, including its comments on genocide, should be taken as the last word on the subject. Indeed, it's specifically stated in Section 2 of the report entitled "Applicable Law," and that's in I11, part I11 of Annex 3, and I quote paragraph 41. And here's where I've been told, Your Honours, that I must slow down, when I'm on these quotes. So I intend to, with your permission. "The commission that has chosen to comment on selected legal issues because of their particular significance for understanding the legal context relating to violations of international humanitarian law committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. The Commission's mandate is to provide the Secretary-General with its conclusions on the evidence of such violations and not provide an analysis of the legal issues. It will be for the International Tribunal to make legal findings in connection with particular cases." I should add that two cases decided by this Tribunal have already called into question one of the findings of the Commission of Experts. A considerable part of the Commission of Experts' report had to do with the events in the Prijedor region of Bosnia. The commission had concluded - and this is in section I41, paragraph 182; it concluded as follows - "It is unquestionable that the events in Opstina Prijedor since 30 April 1992 qualify as crimes against humanity. Furthermore, it is likely to be confirmed under due process of law that these events constitute genocide." The events in Prijedor, particularly in the Keraterm and Omarska concentration camps have been the subject of litigation before this Tribunal, notably in the Sikirica case and the Stakic case. In both cases, the Trial Chamber, after carefully considering the evidence, ruled that they were indeed crimes against humanity committed but that the events involved did not constitute genocide, contrary to the suggestion contained in the report of the Commission of Experts. The Commission's report was based on events which occurred during the period of its existence, from 1992 through 1994. The Commission conducted a number of on-site investigations, including mass grave exhumations in Vukovar and in other areas, rape and sexual assault investigations, the Battle of Dubrovnik investigation, investigation of ethnic cleansing in Prijedor, as I said before, and others. It was in this context of murders, destruction of property, and ethnic cleansing that the Commission compiled its report. Not long after its report was submitted, the former chairman of the Commission, Professor Bassiouni, wrote an article in the Criminal Law Forum -- it's Volume V, starting at page 279. And by the way, we didn't reproduce that. Looking back now, I wish we had. But I think it's okay because the Prosecutor has in its many attachments includes a book by Professor Bassiouni "The Law of the Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia" and it's in the Prosecutor's attachments. And that part from the International Law Journal is quoted right there. And here's what Professor Bassiouni had to say. He said, "With respect to the crime of genocide, the Commission took the position that the definition of this crime in the Genocide Convention of 1948 is not static. Rather, the definition is sufficiently pliable to encompass not only the targeting of an entire group as stated in the Convention, but also the targeting of certain segments of a given group, such as the Muslim elite or Muslim women." Our argument here is that, with all respect to Professor Bassiouni, it is evident that by claiming that the definition of genocide was not static and was sufficiently pliable to include the targeting of certain sections of a given group, Professor Bassiouni and also the Commission of Experts has given an overly broad definition to the crime of genocide and, in our submission, has paid insufficient respect to the dictates of the 1948 Genocide Convention and its commentaries. Nowhere in the lengthy Commission of Experts report is there any analysis of the provisions of the 1948 Genocide Convention, as I have previously related to this Appeals Chamber. I suggest that the Commission of Experts had a thesis to expound, and that is this: That the definition of the crime, that the definition of genocide, should be liberally interpreted to cover as both genocide and crimes against humanity the incidents of murder, violation, and ethnic cleansing which took place in the former Yugoslavia during the period 1992 through 1994 and presumably thereafter. Our submission is that, to the contrary, the definition of genocide and the evolution of the different drafts of the Genocide Convention unmistakably show that the drafters of the Genocide Convention made genocidal acts solely -- acts aimed slowly at the physical or biological destruction of the group. The convention specifically eliminated the proposal of Professor Lempkin, that the forced and systematic exile of individuals representing the leadership of the group should constitute genocide. They specifically rejected that. The killing of the leaders of the group, the elite of the group, as characterised by Professor Bassiouni in his article that I quoted, relate, if at all, to that portion of the genocide statute, which as originally written at the draft convention would have prohibited acts aimed at "preventing the preservation or development" of the group. There's no question that killing the leaders of a group or its military personnel, which is further suggested in the Trial Chamber's opinion, could certainly in the short run affect the "preservation or development" of the group. But this language was eliminated by the ad hoc committee and the final draft covered acts aimed solely at physical or biological destruction. Moreover, we note that some respected commentators have criticised the rationale of the Commission of Experts that one can legitimately base a finding of genocide on destruction of the group's leadership. Mr. Payam Akhavan, formerly the Chief Legal Advisor for the Office of the Prosecutor at the ICTY, wrote in 1998 in an article submitted to the American Society of International Law to note the 50th-year anniversary of the passage of the 1948 Genocide Convention, as follows, and this is in Part K, page 11 of Annex 3: It has also been suggested," said Mr. Akhavan, "that the destruction of a relatively small number or proportion of a group should qualify as genocide when those destroyed constitute the intellectual, political, religious, or other leadership element of a group. The destruction of a group's leadership, it is argued, represents a loss to the group that is disproportionate to the actual numbers killed. The problem with this functional approach is the implicit, arguably elitist, assumption that the lives of individuals with a particular status are more important than the lives of others to the survival of a group." By the same token, Professor William Schabas, in his November 2000 article in the Fordham International Law Journal, cited and attached to our appeal brief, which we've mentioned before, stated as follows: "The significant-part approach inevitably leads to speculation about what the killing of one or the other strata in a community will do to its survival. Perhaps killing the leaders will do the trick. But somebody bent on destroying a group might more logically focus on the children or the women, as they ensure the group's survival. And this results in value judgements about how important one or another group may be to the survival of the community." In Jelisic, the Trial Chamber held that Jelisic killed at random and without a particular intent to destroy the Bosnian Muslims as a group. According to the Trial Chamber in Jelisic, it might be possible to infer the requisite genocidal intent from the "desired destruction of a more limited number of persons selected for the impact that their disappearance would have on the survival of the group as such," citing as authority for this proposition, of course, the report of the Commission of Experts. Ultimately, the Trial Chamber found that it was not possible "to conclude beyond all reasonable doubt that the choice of victims arose from a precise logic to destroy the most representative figures of the Muslim community in Brcko to the point of threatening the survival of that community." The Appeals Chamber held that the evidence was sufficient to warrant a finding of genocide but really didn't expound significantly on the substantive law relating to genocide. In Sikirica, the Court concluded that the intent to destroy a substantial number of Bosnian Muslims or Bosnian Croats could not properly be inferred and that the case was really one of ethnic cleansing which did not cross the line from persecution to genocide. On the qualitative aspect of the case, the Sikirica Chamber held that the killing of a limited number of Bosnian Muslims who had acted in defence of their villages would not significantly impact the survival of the Bosnian Muslim population as a whole in Prijedor. So in neither Jelisic or Sikirica did the decision on the so-called qualitative aspect of genocide constitute the ratio de decidendi of the case. It was not, if I understand that Latin term correctly, the "reason why the case was decided as it was," citing from Judge Shahabuddeen's recent separate opinion in the Ojdanic case. Nor has there been an Appellate Chamber decision on whether the qualitative test, as proposed by the Commission of Experts and adopted by the Trial Chamber, should be used in determining whether genocide has been committed. In short, I believe that the significant part qualitative approach recommended by the Commission of Experts is not embedded in the law of the Tribunal to this point, and I respectfully suggest that it should not be. I should add that even if the Appeals Chamber were to deem it appropriate to consider the qualitative approach set forth in the Commission of Experts' report, we submit that the result would still not warrant a finding of genocidal intent in this case. There was no evidence introduced at the Krstic trial that Bosnian Serb forces sought to eliminate the leadership of the group. As Mr. Schabas stated in his law review article - and I quote - "But in Krstic, where the victims were men and boys of military age, there was no real suggestion that they were community leaders or representative figures. Indeed, it would seem likely that the leaders of the community would be men above" - and that's italicised - "above military age. There was unchallenged evidence that General Krstic had organised the transfer of women, children, and the elderly from the Srebrenica area so that they would not be affected by the coming holocaust. Did General Krstic also transfer the wise old leaders of the community? The judgement doesn't say." And nor was there ever any evidence introduced by the Prosecution at the trial on that issue. In its opinion, the Trial Chamber does state that "extermination specifically directed against law enforcement and military personnel" may affect a significant section of the group in that its renders the group at large defenceless against other abuses of a similar or other nature - again, quoting verbatim from the Commission of Experts' report. We note first that the elderly men, women, and children were safely transported out of Srebrenica during the period 11 and 12 July 1995 before the mass killings of the Bosnian Muslim military-aged men began. Second, there is no reason why law enforcement and military personnel should be treated any differently from other so-called significant sections or leaders of the community. Indeed, since it is the business of law enforcement and military personnel to be involved in battles and war, there is less reason, we suggest, to single them out from the significant section of the civilian population. In Sikirica, the Trial Chamber rejected the submission of the Prosecution that all those Bosnian Muslims who were active in the resistance of the takeover of their villages should be treated a leaders. Said the Court in Sikirica, "acceptance of that submission would necessarily involve a definition of leadership so elastic as to be meaningless." Further, according to the Trial Chamber, the death of the Bosnian Muslim men "precluded any attempt by the Bosnian Muslims to recapture the territory." Paragraph 595. As shown in earlier submissions, the crime of genocide, the crime of crimes, is not about making an impact on part of a group or eliminating part of a group's ability to live in a specific area or, indeed, to recapture the area. The offence requires an intent to destroy the group in whole or in part as such, and that conclusion was one that could not be justified by the evidence presented to the Trial Chamber. Finally, Your Honours, I'd like to turn to the question of General Krstic individually. The Trial Chamber held that there was a joint criminal enterprise to commit genocide. The Trial Chamber also held that General Krstic shared that genocidal intent. We believe strongly that that was error. As a backdrop in determining General Krstic's intent, I should like to begin our discussion by reviewing when and under what circumstances the plan to kill all of the Bosnian Muslim men was conceived. As the Trial Chamber noted - paragraph 360 - "The Prosecution built its case on the theory that the plan to execute the Bosnian Muslim men of Srebrenica was devised in the evening hours of 11 July and the early morning hours of 12 July 1995, once the VRS became aware of the presence of men amongst the crowd at Potocari." At that time, it is undisputed that General Krstic was not the corps commander but the chief of staff to the corps commander, General Zivanovic. The Prosecution contended that the execution plan, given its scale and level of detailed organisation involved, must have been conducted as a "military operation" and that General Krstic was involved in the development of the plan from the outset. That's paragraph 361. This argument was specifically rejected by the Trial Chamber as follows - again, paragraph 361: "The Trial Chamber does not accept this argument. Whereas there is ample direct evidence showing that General Krstic was involved in organising matters relating to the transportation of the Bosnian Muslim women, children, and elderly out of Potocari, there is no corresponding evidence showing him involved in making arrangements for the executions. He was not seen or heard giving any orders that could be construed as arranging the detention sites, guards, blindfolds, ligatures, or other matters relating specifically to the executions. To the contrary, during this period General Krstic was engaged as the commander for the operation at Zepa, which was marshal and a new forward command post to establish. The fact that General Krstic, along with several units of the Drina Corps, was concentrating on Zepa just as the plan for the Srebrenica executions went into operation, suggest that the plan to kill the Bosnian Muslim men was not conceived as a military operation to be primarily implemented by the Drina Corps." Rather, the Trial Chamber concluded that on the basis of the evidence, the "Trial Chamber cannot discount the possibility that the execution plan was initially devised by members of the VRS Main Staff without consultation with the Drina Corps command generally and General Krstic in particular. That's paragraph 362 of the judgement. The recently admitted additional evidence submitted by the Defence - and that's tabs 1, 2, and 3, attached to the Rule 115 motion - corroborates the Trial Chamber's finding that the Drina Corps and General Krstic in particular had little to do with the capture of the thousands of Bosnian Muslim men which took place on 13 July 1995. The Zvornik police reports, received by the Defence well after the judgement in the case, show that the capture and attempted liquidation of about 8.000 Muslim soldiers, as stated in the police report, was being done solely by MUP units "without the cooperation or assistance from VRS in blocking and annihilation of the huge number of enemy soldiers." So having stated that the capture and annihilation of the Bosnian Muslim men were primarily a Main Staff operation, without the assistance of the Drina Corps as of 13 July 1995, how did the Trial Chamber conclude that "by the evening of 13 July at the latest, General Krstic knew that the Muslim men were being executed at a number of separate sites"? This was the basis for the Trial Chamber's conclusion - and I quote - "On 13 July, when he was preparing the military operation at Zepa which commenced the next day, General Krstic found out that thousands of men were fleeing in the column toward the woods towards Tuzla, thousands of Srebrenica men were fleeing in the column toward the woods towards Tuzla and had been captured on the territory of the Drina Corps. As the then-corps chief of staff, "the primary coordinator of the corps activity," General Krstic must have been aware that no adequate measures were being taken to provide for shelter, food, water, and medical care for several thousand captured men and that no arrangements or negotiations were ongoing for their prisoner-of-war camp -- prisoner-of-war exchange." The Trial Chamber concluded - and I quote, paragraph 622 - "On that basis alone, the Trial Chamber must conclude that by the evening of 13 July at the latest, General Krstic knew that the Muslim men were being executed at a number of separate sites and that none had been allowed to enter government-held territory along with the women, children, and elderly. General Krstic could only surmise that the original objective of ethnic cleansing by forcible transfer had turned into a lethal plan to destroy the male population of Srebrenica once and for all." As we've stated in our brief, the Trial Chamber could just as easily have reached what we regard as the more logical conclusion and one consistent with the presumption of innocence, and that is that General Krstic would have known that the prisoners were not given proper care and treatment, given the lack of facilities and manpower to do so. The evidence showed that the capture and detention of the men was primarily an MUP staff operation by the Main Staff. Why should the Trial Chamber, as Mr. Schabas put it in his Law Review article at page 50, have "presumed" that General Krstic knew of the summary executions solely because there were inadequate facilities to house and care for the number of Bosnian Muslim men who had been captured by MUP forces? This is just one of the many presumptions that the Trial Chamber engaged in as to General Krstic's individual liability; as I mentioned the other day, we've set them forth in detail on pages 31 and 32 of our appellant brief, and I will visit one of them a little bit later on. Here again, the Trial Chamber did not, as required by the Delalic appeal decision, adopt the conclusion from the evidence that was consistent with innocence. The conclusion reached by the Trial Chamber, we respectfully suggest, certainly was not the "only reasonable conclusion available" under the Delalic rationale. The question to be determined is whether the Prosecution proved beyond a reasonable doubt that General Krstic intended to destroy in part the Bosnian Muslim group as such. Our submission is that there was neither direct nor circumstantial evidence which showed that General Krstic intended to destroy what the Trial Chamber held to be a distinct part of the Bosnian Muslim group; that is to say, the Bosnian Muslims at Srebrenica. The majority of the Bosnian Muslims at Srebrenica -- some 15.000 to 25.000 women, children, and elderly men -- were transported by bus from Srebrenica to Bosnian Muslim territory under strict orders by General Krstic that "not a hair on their head should be harmed." This was consistent with General Krstic's reputation for humane treatment which characterised his entire military career, as we have set forth in detail in our brief, and was noted to be true by the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber specifically found, at paragraph 420, that "General Krstic appears as a reserved and serious career officer who is unlikely to have ever instigated a plan such as the one devised for the mass execution of Bosnian Muslim men following the takeover of Srebrenica in July 1995. Left to his own devices, it seems doubtful that General Krstic would have been associated with such a plan at all." General Krstic testified for a number of days at the trial. After hearing and observing General Krstic, the Trial Chamber made the following conclusions, at paragraph 724 - and I quote - "The Trial Chamber's overall assessment is that General Krstic is a professional soldier who willingly participated in the forcible transfer of all women, children, and elderly from Srebrenica but would not likely, on his own, have embarked on a genocidal venture. His own commander, General Mladic, was calling the shots and personally supervising the killings. General Krstic's participation in the genocide consisted primarily of allowing Drina Corps assets to be used in connection with the executions from 14 July onwards and assisting with the provision of men to be deployed to participate in executions that occurred on 16 July 1995. General Krstic remained largely passive in the face of knowledge of what was going on. When pressured, he assisted the effort to deploying some men for the task, but on his own, he would not likely have initiated such a plan." We suggest that the language of the Trial Chamber almost standing alone refutes the idea that General Krstic intended to commit genocide. "One who remains largely passive," in the words of the Trial Chamber, can hardly be equated to one who has the genocidal intent to destroy a group of human beings. The Nazis were not largely passive. The extermination of the Jews and the Gypsies and others was their passion. The same is true with the Hutu extermination of the Tutsis in Rwanda, where those ordering and taking part in the killings did so with fervour and vengeance, specifically to eliminate every man, woman, and child they could find with the Tutsi population. In addition, the Trial Chamber said that "when pressured" General Krstic assisted in the effort of deploying some men to the task, clearly referring to the allegation that General Krstic assisted in the executions at Branjevo Farm -- and then by implication, the later executions at Pilica Dom, allegedly by the same people -- by making arrangements for members of the Bratunac Brigade to assist in those executions. As Mr. Petrusic will shortly argue, the Prosecution never proved beyond a reasonable doubt -- in our submission, they never proved at all -- that General Krstic ever dispatched any member from the Bratunac Brigade to aid in these executions. We think the evidence is overwhelming on that in our favour. But the point here is that even if the Appeals Chamber should adopt that finding - we certainly hope you don't, but even if you do adopt it - it shows at most General Krstic's knowledge that Bosnian Muslim men were being executed. It does not show a genocidal intent to destroy a part of the Bosnian Muslim group as such. The Trial Chamber found that the conversation between General Krstic and Colonel Beara, the Main Staff officer, to be the "aggressive apex" of General Krstic's participation in the killing plan. The conversation clearly supports the Defence argument that General Krstic did not agree with the actions of the Main Staff. The Trial Chamber found that General Krstic's statement to Colonel Beara, "You guys fucked me up so much," was evidence that the Main Staff was "primarily directing the executions, albeit calling upon the resources of the Drina Corps command." When coupled with his next comment to Colonel Beara that "Fuck it, now I'll be the one to blame," it is evident that General Krstic did not have a desire to execute prisoners, let alone an intent to commit genocide, but the quite prescient belief that he would be blamed for it even though it was an Main Staff action that he wanted no part of. The Appeals Chamber will recall that in that conversation, General Krstic referred Colonel Beara to other sources for supplying the men needed, including the MUP, and finally stated without any commitment, "I'll see what I can do." Again, our submission is that General Krstic did nothing after this conversation to furnish any men from the Bratunac Brigade to assist in the executions. But again, if the Appeals Chamber finds that he did, the assistance was reluctant in the extreme. The Trial Chamber correctly characterised General Krstic's conduct as "largely passive" and correctly stated that if he did take part in supplying men for the executions, he did so "when pressured." How does reluctant and passive participation amount to genocidal intent, an intent to destroy a part of the Bosnian Muslim group as such? Our respectful submission is that it does not, and we ask the Appeals Chamber to reverse the Trial Chamber's finding that General Krstic intended to commit genocide. Our submission is that the Trial Chamber's interpretation of the genocide statute violates two fundamental legal principles: First, the Trial Chamber's interpretation is inconsistent with the principle of in dubio pro re which provides that as to the case of doubt as to the content or meaning of a statute or rule, the interpretation most favourable to the accused should be adopted. And I refer to the more recent decision in the Ojdanic opinion, paragraph 27. Nowhere is this better illustrated than in the Trial Chamber's conclusion, based on the Commission of Experts' report, that deportation of the men, women, and children was considered an act of genocide because it results in the disappearance of the Bosnian Muslim community in Srebrenica. We suggest that, to the contrary, the principle in dubio pro re, if not actual logic, leads to an opposite conclusion, that the transfer of the women, children, and elderly from Srebrenica proves not the commission of genocide but an intention to avoid committing genocide. Second, we suggest that the Trial Chamber's interpretation of the genocide statute is contrary to the principle of nullum crimen sine lege. Most importantly, the application of this principle requires that the Tribunal should apply rules of international humanitarian law which are beyond any doubt part of customary law. Certainly, as of July 1995, when the events at Srebrenica took place, the principles espoused by the Trial Chamber were not beyond any doubt part of international customary law, particularly as it relates to equating displacement of a population with genocide. In the recent Ojdanic decision of 21 May 2003, the Appeals Chamber, explaining the principle nullum crimen sine lege, stated as follows: "The Tribunal must further be satisfied that the criminal liability in question was sufficiently foreseeable and that the law providing for such liability must be sufficiently accessible at the relevant time for it to warrant a criminal conviction and sentencing under the head of responsibility selected by the Prosecution." We suggest that the Trial Chamber's interpretation of the genocide statute does not comport with this principle. Our point is this: Genocide is specifically made criminal in Article -- by Article 4 and condemns the destruction of a group by the various means listed. Deportation or forcible transfer is not listed as one of those means of perpetration. Deportation is specifically set out as a crime against humanity under Article 5. Since there was nothing in the genocide statute to indicate that deportation or forcible transfer -- other than the forcible transfer of children -- again, since there was nothing in the genocide statute to indicate that deportation or forcible transfer could also be considered an act of genocide, we suggest that the principle of nullum crimen sine lege prevented the Trial Chamber from, in the words of the Ojdanic case, "creating new law or from interpreting existing law beyond the reasonable limits of acceptable clarification." Our final submission that under the evidence presented to the Trial Chamber, General Krstic is not guilty of genocide. By making this argument, neither General Krstic nor his lawyers are attempting to minimise the gravity of what happened at Srebrenica. Indeed, we agree with the introductory comments of the Trial Chamber in the Krstic case, when the Chamber stated - and I quote - "The events of the nine days from 10th to 19th July 1995 in Srebrenica defy description in their horror and their implications for humankind's capacity to revert to acts of brutality under the stresses of conflict." Horrible and despicable as the acts of Srebrenica were, our submission is that the evidence did not warrant a finding by the Trial Chamber that there was a joint criminal enterprise which intended to commit genocide at Srebrenica or that General Krstic ever had that intent. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sepenuk. I believe that your colleague now would like to continue the argument. And I give him the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, first of all, Your Honours. And before I begin my submission, with your permission, Mr. President, I should like to move to this other rostrum so that you wouldn't get the impression that I am hiding behind this pillar from the members of the Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My learned colleague, Mr. Sepenuk, in the course of his submissions yesterday and today, mentioned on several occasions that members of the Bratunac Brigade did not take part in the executions at the Branjevo Farm, nor at the Pilica cultural centre. What makes this important is that members of the Bratunac Brigade -- or rather, the Bratunac Brigade is a subordinate unit to General Krstic and its commander, Colonel Blagojevic, was directly subordinated to General Krstic. Regarding this submission of the Defence, that is, there is no evidence that members of the Bratunac Brigade participated in the executions at these two locations; however, the Trial Chamber came to the opposite conclusion in interpreting the intercept, the exhibit of the Prosecution, C22, and I would like to remind you that it is a conversation between Colonel Rasic in the command of the Drina Corps and Lieutenant Colonel Popovic, who is somewhere around Zvornik. In a part of that intercept, Lieutenant Colonel Popovic says that "This commander is up there; up there had some terrible problems and that Vidoje Blagojevic's men did not arrive on time." The Judges of the Trial Chamber adopted the position that these were members of the Bratunac Brigade, on the basis of the interpretation given by Mr. Butler, that is, an interpretation of the phrase "up there," saying that this referred to -- that this referred to an area north of Zvornik, that is, Pilica. This is transcript page 5144. The Trial Chamber further found, in paragraph 401 and 402, that the conversation and the interpretation of it given by Mr. Butler was consistent with the testimony of Drazen Erdemovic, who testified on the 21st of May, 2000 in the Trial Chamber. On page 3132, Mr. Erdemovic stated that "The executions at the Branjevo Farm started around 10.00 on the 16th of July and that they were continued in the Pilica centre in the afternoon of that same day." Mr. Erdemovic also testified that around 1.00 or 2.00 of the 16th of July certain men arrived from Bratunac to assist in the executions. Mr. Erdemovic at the time, even in response to a question of one of the members of the Trial Chamber who asked him to identify those men, he didn't identify them as being members of the Bratunac Brigade. He simply said, "Those were men from Bratunac. They were wearing a military uniform." Therefore, linking this phrase "up there" with Erdemovic's testimony, Mr. Butler asserted that these were members of the Bratunac Brigade and the Trial Chamber made its findings on that basis. Today, with the evidence presented by the Defence in its brief on the 24th of November, 2003, and on the basis of the testimony of Mr. Butler in the Blagojevic case regarding this same incident, we now have quite a different interpretation by Mr. Butler. On transcript page 4617, in the annex of our Brief A - and this is the transcript from the Blagojevic case, in answer to the Prosecutor's question, Mr. McCloskey: "In your testimony, Mr. Butler, did you make an error when testifying in the Krstic case regarding information from Mr. Erdemovic?" Mr. Butler stated, "Yes, I did. I recognised it when I reviewed my testimony. As soon as I saw what I had said, I asked the tape to be checked because I allegedly said that they were men from the Bratunac Brigade. And I would like to say for the record that from the beginning of my connection with this case, I always knew that Erdemovic had always said that those were men or soldiers from Bratunac. He never said that they were men from the Bratunac Brigade." Further interpretations of Mr. Butler's testimony led to a question by the Prosecutor to explain the meaning of the sentence in this intercept, when Rasic asked Popovic - and I quote - "Tell me whether anything has arrived from Vidoje Blagojevic." Mr. Butler concluded that "In view of the other information we acquired, where various units were asked to send additional troops to the Zvornik Brigade area." Butler goes on to explain, "Rasic asks whether those troops had been sent and whether those who should have been sent from Bratunac had arrived"; transcript page 4618. Further on, Butler points to the conclusion that a group of soldiers from Bratunac had finally arrived and had been sent up there, that they had been sent in the direction of the forward command post in the Bajkovica area of the Zvornik. So locations where combat operations were ongoing, locations where during the 16th of July aid was requested for units engaged in combat operations and certainly not in executions. Another phrase which has caused some doubts and erroneous conclusions in Mr. Butler's explanation and during the trial of General Krstic is the interpretation of the phrase "up there," and all in this context of this intercept. This phrase, according to the interpretation of Dragan Obrenovic given during his testimony on the 6th of October, 2003 - transcript page 2601 - and explaining this same intercept, Mr. Obrenovic stated - I quote - "I think this refers to the Bajkovica area, where most of the conflict was going on in that area." On page 2678 of the transcript of the 7th of October, Obrenovic goes on to say, "If you expect me to give my opinion as to what Lieutenant Colonel Popovic meant, I've already given my opinion. I believe that he was referring to Bajkovica, the area of the 4th Battalion where combat was ongoing." Obrenovic removes all doubt by stating that Lieutenant Colonel Popovic, had he wanted to refer to Pilica, he would have said "down there," because the Drina River flows towards Pilica, so that is the downstream direction. Clearly Lieutenant Colonel, when he says up there -- Lieutenant Colonel Popovic -- he means Bajkovica. And to round off this point, in his final analysis of this conversation, Mr. Butler, on page 4717, says that he's ready to conclude that those were not men from the Bratunac Brigade involved in the execution at the Branjevo Farm and Pilica. And again, on page 4736, that the most correct conclusion to be inferred is that "up there" actually referred to the area of the forward command post at Bajkovica. Those would be my submissions regarding this intercept on which the Trial Chamber, in paragraphs 401 and 402, found that members of the Bratunac Brigade participated in the executions at Branjevo and Pilica. Your Honours, the submission of General Krstic's Defence is that General Krstic's guilt begins and ends on the 12th of July in Potocari. If the Chamber finds and accepts that he was a participant in the joint criminal enterprise, then in the submission of the Defence he can be considered that only for the time period and the activities related to forcible transfer in Potocari. The intercepts and the evidence in this case point to the fact that he undertook certain steps when he received information and took steps to organise the buses. Yesterday my colleague said that his role was a minor one in that operation, and I would agree with that. General Krstic has a very high rank, but the circumstances and the situation and the acts that he took really do place him at a very low level. The intercepts show that he was enquiring whether the buses were coming, whether they had arrived, where they were. It is a fact that in Potocari on the 12th of July he spent about one to two hours, according to the finding of the Trial Chamber, but one should not lose from sight that after that -- which means not late than 3.00 p.m. on the 12th of July -- he left that area and that he did not return there again. One should also not lose from sight that at the relevant time for the forcible transfer of the population he issued an order that not a hair should be hurt on the head of any single one of those civilians, and I would be free to assert that this was a much stricter, a much stronger, a much more emphatic order stated in that intercept than any other written order. In the opinion of the Defence, Your Honours, by issuing such an order, he is disassociating himself from all the activities which were engaged in subsequently. Could he have done anything more than that except to issue an order to subordinate units that no member of the Muslim nation should be hurt or treated, contrary to the customs of war and contrary to the provisions of the Geneva Conventions? He stated this very clearly. General Krstic's departure from that area shows that his basic involvement was with the combat operations around the other enclave. The Prosecutor asserted, during yesterday's hearing, that resources of the Drina Corps were used and that he must have known about that and he should have taken steps to prevent that, referring to resources of the Zvornik Brigade, and those resources of the Zvornik Brigade were two machines, ULT 220, and a machine known as BGH 700 used in the burial at Orahovac. Could he -- could General Krstic have known this? In the submission of the Defence, he did not. And as proof of such a submission, the Defence offers General Krstic's overall behaviour and also an intercepted conversation dated the 17th of July, when General Krstic requested the troops under his command located in Vlasenica. And the conversation went as follows: "Krstic: Bring me the soldiers you have immediately. "X: About four. "Krstic: How many? And he says, "I only have the guards. I'm involved up there -- "Krstic: I beg your pardon? "X: I'm busy up there." Then a word that is unclear. "Here where we were before. "Krstic: "Where before? Fuck you." And X says: "I have -- Osmaci. I have three more soldiers and three on guard here. I have three. "Under whose permission did you send troops down there," says Krstic. "X: "By orders from the Main Staff." "Krstic: "Fuck you. Return those soldiers to me as soon as possible down there." One can conclude from this intercepted conversation that the Main Staff, without any permission and without any knowledge or without informing subordinate commanders, is taking and using resources at will. Your Honours, it is very hard to speak of punishment if the Defence position is known from the very beginning, that is, the Initial Appearance of General Krstic, when he entered a plea of not guilty. During the trial itself, General Krstic and his Defence upheld that position. Today we are in a situation when the Defence says that if this Honourable Chamber comes to the conclusion and determines the existence of General Krstic's guilt, it can relate to forcible transfer in Potocari. And with regard to that segment, the Defence submits that the initial sentence should be significantly reduced. Your Honours, that would complete the submissions of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrusic. I see we still have 20 minutes before the break, and I'm sure that my colleagues and myself would want to ask some questions. If I may start with a number of questions to Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk, do you agree with the Trial Chamber's conclusion in paragraph 560 of the judgement that "The Bosnian Muslims of Srebrenica or Eastern Bosnia are a part of the protected group of all Bosnian Muslims within the meaning of the term 'genocide'"? What are you arguing? That this part is not substantial enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: What we're arguing, Your Honour that, the criteria adopted by the Trial Chamber was to determine if -- if General Krstic destroyed a part of a part of the Bosnian Muslims. In other words, they held that the destruction of 7500 men out of the Bosnian Muslim group in Srebrenica, together with the deportation of the rest of the people, constitutes an intention to commit genocide. We say that the Trial Chamber should have compared that number against the whole of the Bosnian Muslim group, and they would have reached a different conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So you are in fact arguing that the part of the population of Bosnian Muslims, as referred to by the Trial Chamber is that paragraph, the Bosnian Muslims of Srebrenica are not a substantial enough part of all Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, I think -- Your Honour, I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I'm trying to narrow it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I understand. And I -- the language of the -- of the Trial Chamber in Stakic I think is -- is very good on this point. I think we've reached a time in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal that it's fruitless to argue that you cannot have genocide in a limited geographical area. The Akayesu case held in a burgomaster -- whatever that expression is; and there have been a number of courts that have held and indeed commentators who have also mentioned that you can have genocide in a limited geographical area. But again, as the Trial Chamber noted in Stakic, it can create problems, in terms of -- of limiting it to certain -- I mean, can you have -- can you have genocide in a village? Can you have genocide in an area with 100 people, whatnot? But I'm willing to accept for purposes of this case, the definition of the Trial Chamber. But we claim that even defining the group as the Bosnian Muslims of Srebrenica, there's no genocide because -- because for one thing, most of the group was deported from Srebrenica, showing, in our view, an overall intention to commit ethnic cleansing and certainly not an intention to destroy the Bosnian Muslim group as such. The 7500 men were destroyed, in our view, precisely because they were military-age men and not because they were Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I -- I will turn to that aspect of the military men -- military-age character of the Bosnian Muslim men in Srebrenica in a moment. But let me stay for just one more second on this question of substantial part, because yesterday you argued this extensively. You have pointed out to us -- to us repeatedly the need to adhere strictly to the language of the Statute by implication -- by reference to the Genocide Convention. Now, Article 4 of the Statute does not refer anywhere to a substantial part. Where do you take it from?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I believe, Your Honour, that that's the gloss that's been added by the cases. I think I've read -- I hope I've read every case in this area. I've also read the commentary. I've read the International Law Commission, Whitaker, all the commentators. And the case law; Jelisic, Sikirica. I don't think it was particularly referred to in Stakic because of the comments about demography and what, although I could be wrong about that. But -- but that is a gloss that's been added to the genocide statute because the very nature of genocide itself, that there must be an intention to destroy a substantial part -- and every case, to my knowledge, in this Chamber and in the Rwanda Chamber - although, there they simply say -- I believe the language in the Rwanda Chamber is "a considerable number of individuals." But in this Chamber, the term is used, yes, "a substantial part."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. You realise, of course, that Jelisica and Sikirica, that those aspects were only discussed by Trial Chambers and not by the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Now, let's continue this clarification. In paragraph 594, the Trial Chamber found that the Bosnian Serb forces sought to eliminate all of the Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica and in surrounding areas as a community. The means by which this was to be achieved was by killing all the Bosnian Muslim men of military age in that community. Was it unreasonable for the Trial Chamber to conclude that if all the military-aged men in Srebrenica and surrounding areas were killed, the Bosnian Muslims in that area would not continue to exist?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, first of all, as I pointed out, the -- the civilians left first; the women, the children, the elderly, left on the 11th and 12th. So I don't think that Defence argument particularly holds. Also, when they talked about the annihilation of the Bosnian Muslim community in Srebrenica, there's only five ways to commit genocide, as Your Honour well knows: The term is destruction, and the way to destroy the group is by the five methods listed in the Statute. And what the -- what happened in this case - put it at the most basic - 7500 men were killed; the balance of the people were deported. Now, that could constitute annihilation of the community, but it doesn't constitute the killing or the other acts mentioned by the genocide statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's turn back, then, to the killing. You seem to argue that the fact that women were not killed shows that genocide was not committed because killing women would have been a more effective way of destroying the procreative capacity of the Bosnian Muslim community. But why couldn't the Trial Chamber conclude that killing just of the military-age men was an equally effective way of achieving that goal?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Because the military-age men, I don't think, constitute part of the Bosnian Muslim group as such. There's another reason for killing the military-age men, aside from wanting to eliminate the Bosnian Muslim group as such. And again, the safe treatment of the women and children and elderly belie an intent to destroy the group as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: But if you add up the destruction of all men basically of procreative age in the area of Srebrenica, you add up to that that women and children were forced to leave that area. Does this not add up to the destruction of Bosnian Muslims in the area of Srebrenica, which was regarded by the Trial Chamber as a destruction of the part of the protected community?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All it had, Your Honour, is it had what may have been a lasting impact on the Bosnian Muslims of Srebrenica. But the women and children and elderly remained alive, remained able to procreate. The group could have been eventually reconstituted. But again, that's not the question. The question was: Were they destroyed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: The community was destroyed, if you take these two components into -- into effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, certainly if you take the two. But our submission is that the only component that this Chamber can legitimately consider is the killing, and not the deportation. If you are going to consider the deportation, I would think the presumption of innocence and the Delalic rationale about accepting the only legal conclusion from the evidence is that the deportation of the women, children, and elderly show and an avoidance of an attempt to commit genocide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll now turn to my colleagues. Judge Schomburg, please. Judge Schomburg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Sorry to come back to the question of applicable law. Today's transcript, page 5, you mentioned again the report of experts and the opinion given by Professor Bassiouni that genocide would not be a static crime. The question goes to both parties: What is the applicable law? Do we have to apply the Convention of 1948 as such or is there any discernible development of the term or the offence of genocide since then, based on the implementation of the Genocide Convention? I personally did not find a persuasive common approach in the implementation of the Genocide Convention as such. Related to the Genocide Convention as such, I can only find that the United States ratified the Genocide Convention in 1986. It adopted an understanding, which reads that "The term intent to destroy in whole or in part a national, ethnical, racial, or religious group as such, appearing in Article 2, means the specific intent to destroy in whole or in a substantial part" - to come back to this - "a national, ethnical, racial, or religious group as such by the acts specified in Article 2." And I have not seen - please, both parties correct me if I'm wrong - that no other states have so far any other reservations or understandings in relation to this aspect of the convention. Furthermore, taking into account the fundamental principle of nullum crimen sine lege certa, isn't it to a certain extent a risk to merge the legal term of joint criminal enterprise with the convention as such? Doesn't it water down the clear wording of the convention? The second part of my question is the following: If you would follow this need of having a specific intent - and please understand this only as a judicial hint and applying the right to be heard. We should be aware that just in case one could come or would come to another conclusion, that there was no such intent, you yourself. You yourself yesterday mentioned several times a Trial Chamber saying "General Krstic must have known," "he could have known," and so forth. In the indictment, page 13, we can find that General Krstic was charged with genocide or, alternatively, complicity to commit genocide, punishable under Articles 4(3)(e) and 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. So if one, in theory, could or would come to the conclusion that on a higher level there was this specific intent, the question arises: Was there any complicity in genocide, and what is then the necessary mens rea? We have, especially in our Statute, the problem that on the one-hand side, quoting verbatim the Genocide Convention of 1948, we have complicity in genocide and, I think it's undisputed that also for complicity in genocide, specific intent is needed. However, under our Rules, I note that it is not charged as such; but, however, one could take it as a minor include it in the offence. We have the possibility of convicting a person for aiding and abetting to genocide. Aiding and abetting. The mens rea needed is that what you yourself mentioned, he must have known, he knew, or should have known. In light of this second part of the question - and also this question goes to both parties - what about the relationship between complicity in genocide and aiding and abetting to genocide where on would need only a lower standard of mens rea? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I will say -- I'm going to answer, Your Honour. I hope my answer isn't too simple-minded. I hope I've grasped the nuances of your question. But our fundamental premise is that there was no joint criminal enterprise to commit genocide. There was never any intent on the part of a joint criminal enterprise to commit genocide. And nor was there any intent on the part of General Krstic, as I've just stated, so nor was there any complicity in genocide. Nor do we think there was any aiding and abetting of genocide, because again - and I know we've stressed this point greatly in these last few days - is that July 15th conversation with Colonel Beara is the only evidence the government has introduced to indicate that General Krstic could possibly fall within - even as an aider and abettor - we say he's not, because the most he said was "I'll see what I can do," and we're absolutely convinced he did nothing -- more important, whether we're convinced, the evidence shows, we think, beyond any doubt that he did nothing. And as I understand the law of this Tribunal, you must have some concrete action as an aider and abettor. There has to be something to further the enterprise. At the very least, there has to be moral encouragement. I believe that's in the case law. In this case, we don't even have moral encouragement; instead, we have various expletives being used by General Krstic to try to keep Colonel Beara away from him. So certainly in traditional aiding-and-abetting-language, we don't even have that in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: It is 11.00, and we would like today to accommodate the periods of rest of the interpreters properly. We have not finished with the questions. However, I suggest that we rise for half an hour and then continue. And I would like to remind also the Prosecutor that one part of the question of my learned colleague, Judge Schomburg, was directed to the Prosecution. So we will rise for half an hour now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. My learned colleagues will now continue with questions to the Defence. And if I may call on Judge Guney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Mr. Sepenuk, within the framework of the events that took place in Potocari on the 12th of July, there's a point on which I am not quite clear. I hope you will be able to provide some clarification on it. And the point is the following: To organise and provide 50 buses to transfer the Muslim detainees to an uncertain destiny. In other words, an act of such scope, does it necessarily imply the participation in a joint criminal enterprise? In other words, does it imply the knowledge of the goal sought? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Of course, our position is that General Krstic had nothing whatever to do with suggesting the bussing -- the forcible transfer of civilians. He certainly wasn't part of any initial decision to forcibly transfer the civilians. You'll recall the testimony of Mr. Deronjic that, as far as he was concerned, General Krstic was invisible. He didn't even know he was at that Hotel Fontana meeting until he saw a tape afterwards which indicated to him that General Krstic was there. However - and this is where we are paying respect to the Appeals Chamber's rationale in this Tribunal - we felt that given the fact that we could not claim that the Trial Chamber's finding on this forcible transfer point was wholly erroneous, that we could not simply ask the Appeals Chamber to substitute its judgement for the Trial Chamber, and particularly after Your Honours denied our Rule 115 motion with respect to Mr. Deronjic, at least we thought back in those days he was being truthful in his testimony. We now know from Mr. Deronjic's testimony that the options 1, 2, and 3, as he put it, was a smokescreen to cover up the forcible nature of the transfer. But at some point I think the Trial Chamber - again, we -- we have to accept this. We wish we didn't, but I think we do under the Rules of the Chamber and under the Rules of this Tribunal - when General Mladic started to speak, he made it unfortunately clear that there was no real true choice for the civilians to leave the area. At that point, I think the Trial Chamber was warranted in finding that everything from that point on constituted a joint criminal enterprise, at least in terms of who participated to deport the civilians. Our claim is - and again, this is a matter that goes toward sentencing - our claim is that General Krstic was a participant, but there's no evidence that he was any more of an eager participant in this than he was in the -- as he was in that July 15th, 1995 conversation with -- with Colonel Beara. And once he was faced with this, once General Mladic had laid down the law, General Krstic did all he could to make sure that it was a peaceful transfer of civilians. Has that answered your question, Your Honour, or is there ...?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: If Judge Guney would allow me, I would like a small follow-up to his question. Regarding those buses, I think it was mentioned in the argument yesterday that some of these were diverted to transport the male -- the male -- Muslim men. Do you -- can you clarify?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I believe that's correct. I believe there was some diversion of buses at some point to -- for the Bosnian Muslim men. But again, definitely, the whole thrust of the operation was to transport the women, the children, and the elderly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I understand. Is it your argument that General Krstic was not aware of such a diversion of buses?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Oh, no, not at all, Your Honour. No, General Krstic had a great deal to do with the bussing operation in the sentence that he certainly helped organise the buses and that kind of thing. But our argument, again, that we've made earlier, is that that was not an indispensable act here. In other words, anybody, any lower-level office, for goodness sakes, could have arranged for the bussing. It didn't take a general to arrange for the bussing. It so happened in the general scheme of things, with General Mladic calling the shots, General Krstic was designated as the person to help arrange the bussing. But anybody could have arranged the bussing. So certainly, in that sense, General Krstic was not indispensable to that operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now turn to my distinguished colleague Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk, and Mr. Petrusic, I have benefitted enormously from your stimulating submissions, and I would be obliged to you if you would help me on one or two points. Now, arising from what the President has said and from Judge Guney's question, my concern is this: When reference is made to the statement by the appellant that not a hair was to be harmed, to what group of people was the reference directed?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: The women, children, and elderly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, now, Mr. Sepenuk, the question in my mind - and I do believe you can help me - is this: General Krstic was involved in the bussing of women and children, all of them. Does the evidence permit of a reasonable inference being drawn by a reasonable tribunal of fact as to whether he had any intentions for the disposition of the men? And if so, what were those intentions?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. I don't -- I don't believe -- I think that the bussing operation, again, simply showed that General Krstic wanted Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the women, children, and elderly out of Srebrenica as peacefully as possible. And by the way, the dovetailing with Judge Meron's question before, our argument, of course, is that it's not sufficient to show an intent to destroy a community. The intention must be to show to destroy a part of the Bosnian Muslim group as such, not simply the displacement of a community. But getting back to Your Honour's question, the -- I don't really think it showed anything, with respect to the men. If you want to look at an overall genocidal plan, which we claim General Krstic never had - we claim first the joint criminal enterprise didn't have it and, a fortiori, certainly General Krstic never had it - but again, the deportation, forcible transfer of the women, children, and elderly show an intention to avoid killing the Bosnian Muslim group as such. We think the only reasonable inference from the forcible transfer of that group is that it was an intent to avoid the killing of a group as such, not the promotion of the killing. Now, surely it promoted a transfer away from the area. In that sense -- that's the sense the Trial Chamber, used the expression "annihilation." What they meant was -- by " annihilation" was the killing of the 7500 men and the transfer of the 25.000 women, and for reasons that we've stated, we think that was an error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Sepenuk, I wonder if we will make progress by separating the question of law from the question of fact. A question of law which you have raised -- very engagingly, if I may say so -- concerns the proposition that the Prosecution had only proved at most the destruction of part of a part and not part of the whole, as it were. Can we go back to the nub of my question, which is whether the totality of the evidence permits of a reasonable inference being drawn by a reasonable tribunal of fact as to whether the appellant had any intentions for the disposition of the men, as distinguished from the women and children. And if so, what were those intentions?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there's certainly nothing in the trial record that I know of - and I'm going to ask my distinguished colleague, Mr. Petrusic, who was one of the trial lawyers to correct me on this, with Your Honour' permission - there's nothing in the trial record that I know of which indicates any intention whatsoever on General Krstic's part to kill the men, nothing; not a single piece of evidence in the record to indicate an intention by General Krstic concerning the killing of the men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Do you say that that provides scope for returning to Judge Guney's question as to whether in those circumstances a reasonable tribunal of fact could draw an inference as to whether General Krstic was privy to a joint criminal enterprise concerning the disposition of the men?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Again, I -- and please, I -- I hope I'm focussing - and I am focussing on your question, obviously - but there's no evidence that I know of that could attribute that state of mind to General Krstic vis-a-vis the men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. May I turn now to a related aspect. Judge Schomburg referred to the question whether at a higher level there was a certain specific intention. I want you to help me to explore that. Reference has been made to the Fontana meeting being a smokescreen. I take it you'll understand the disposition of the Bench, certainly on my part, to examine whether the letter written by Major General Tolimir on 9th July was itself a smokescreen. By that I have in mind this: In that letter, Major General Tolimir conveyed, I believe, the directives of President Karadzic to the effect that the Geneva Conventions were to be adhered to. Well, now, killings went on between the 13th and the 19th of July and on a large scale. Does the evidence on the part permit a reasonable tribunal of fact to draw an inference to the effect that President Karadzic must have known that these killings were going on?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Do you mean as of July 9th -- I mean -- right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: No, between the 13th and the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That President Karadzic knew what was going on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: First of all, on -- just briefly on the smokescreen point, that letter of July 9th, for all we knew, certainly for all General Krstic knew, was a very legitimate letter, expressing the orders of President Karadzic that, indeed, no civilians were to be harmed and that civilians and military were to be treated in accordance with the Geneva Convention. That changed on the evening of July 11th, the morning of July 12th, when there were men discovered at Potocari and when the Bosnian Muslim column started to escape toward Tuzla. We feel that the Trial Chamber is correct in its holding that's when the killing plan was hatched. And again, we feel there's no evidence whatsoever to connect General Krstic to that. In terms of the knowledge of -- of President Karadzic about those killings during that period, I can only speculate. Of course, we have evidence from Mr. Deronjic that he spoke to President Karadzic and President Karadzic said, "As far as these prisoners are concerned, put them in the Batkovici camp near Bijeljina." In terms of any other evidence from that point on, to show President Karadzic's knowledge, I'm certainly not aware of any. And I ask my colleague, Mr. Petrusic, whether that's correct. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with the Court's indulgence, I should like to follow on to what has just been said in response to the question whether the sequence of events from the meeting of the 12th and the conduct of Mr. Deronjic to reach President Karadzic indicates that on the 13th in the evening, sometime around 200 [sic] hours, we had a conversation with President Karadzic through an intermediary, and in that conversation, via this intermediary Mr. Deronjic addresses the then-President Karadzic and informs him, informs President Karadzic that, in the Bratunac area there were about 2 to 2 and a half thousand male Muslims. Karadzic suggests, once again through this intermediary, that "the goods" - and I quote from the conversation - "should be placed in a warehouse until dawn." Deronjic, for his part, in his testimony, says that he understands as being Karadzic's demand for the Muslim males from Bratunac to be dislocated and taken to the area of Batkovici, which is where certain facilities existed -- or rather, a military prison existed. That's what Deronjic tells us in respect of the destiny of the prisoners of the 13th of July in the evening, those who were put up in Bratunac. Your Honour, in following on from the answer already given by my colleague, I should say that I do not doubt for a single moment that you yourselves have not become informed and acquainted of the substance and indeed the details of this whole proceedings and case, especially when you speak about the existence of joint criminal enterprise and the role played therein by General Krstic. Now, if we're talking about the 12th of July and the meeting at the Fontana Hotel, I should like briefly to draw your attention to the following: We must look at it in continuity, as a continuous process of the meetings being held to discuss the destiny and fate of the Bosnian Muslim civilians who were in Potocari. We had three meetings, in actual fact, which were being held at the level of General Mladic, with representatives of UNPROFOR and the Muslim civilians; two meetings held in the late evening or afternoon and evening hours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, I want to apologise to you very fulsomely in case I have misled you. All I wanted to know was whether from the size of the killings and the duration of the killings there was any evidence from which a reasonable tribunal of fact could make the inference that President Karadzic knew that those killings were going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, looking at the evidence from the case, and that is the testimony of Mr. Deronjic, the Defence of General Krstic holds, and would like to claim, that President Karadzic did not know about the beginning and part of the course that this took, of the killings. Your Honour, the Defence in this case did not delve, nor did the proceedings at court delve into this question in any substantial form, so that the information I have with respect to facts governing that lead me to conclude that the answer to your question would be negative; that is to say, that President Karadzic did not know about the killings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, Mr. Petrusic. Thank you. I have one question of law, I think, for Mr. Sepenuk. Mr. Sepenuk, I was a little -- at one and the same time, I was enthralled and mystified by this submission concerning the proposition that all the Prosecution had proved was that genocide, if it took place, affected only a part of a part of the Muslim population. The impression I have is that you propose a distinction between the Muslim population in Srebrenica and a Muslim population in the whole of Bosnia, and from your point of view what the Prosecution should prove is the destruction of part of the whole Muslim population of Bosnia but that what they had proved was only the destruction of that part of the Muslim population which lay in Srebrenica. Now, that gives me a little difficulty, and I'm sure you can help me, because I'll tell you what is the difficulty that I have: If the Prosecution has proved the destruction of that part of the Muslim population which lay in Srebrenica, would not the Prosecution have logically also proved the destruction of part of the whole Muslim population of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I don't think so, Your Honour. What the Prosecution proved was the destruction of 7500 Bosnian Muslim men and the displacement of 25.000 women, children, and elderly; that's what the Prosecution proved. The Prosecution did not prove the destruction of the distinct part of Srebrenica. The Prosecution only proved the destruction of 7500 men. Now, when I say "only," it gets back to my comment yesterday, Your Honour, about when death and suffering are involved it's repugnant to speak about mathematical calculations, but we have to here. And we feel, again, what was destroyed was 7500 men. The -- the lack of genocidal intent is shown by many things but particularly the safe transport of the women, children, and elderly, and so the Srebrenica community, that section of -- of the chamber which talks about we must look at a distinct part not -- not numbers throughout the country but, rather, a distinct part -- the distinct part was not destroyed. A good number of those people, a great majority of those people were displaced, not destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So if I may perfect my understanding of your submission, it would be this: If - if - the Appeals Chamber were to hold that what was destroyed was a whole Muslim population of Srebrenica through the destruction of the military-aged men, then your submission wouldn't hold that the Prosecution not only proved the destruction of part -- of a part of the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: If you were to hold - and in our view, what you'd have to do was to say that it has to be one of those five ways of committing genocide - if you were to hold that indeed that by virtue of one of those five ways of committing genocide - in this case, killings - that the entire community was indeed destroyed, as it can only be by one of those five methods, then I think we would probably agree with Your Honour, although we might say - and again, I -- by the way, Your Honour, I agree with you; it's -- the words you used were mysterious -- and what was the other word? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I've forgotten it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Right. But it's a very slippery concept. It really is. I mean, I've -- I've wrestled with this now for two years. But again, go back to the Sikirica Chamber too, talking about there still has to be that overall intent to destroy the Bosnian Muslims as a group. And I think that even in the case that Your Honour mentioned there has to be an analysis of all the facts and circumstances, as the Stakic Court recently held, to determine whether the intent was truly to destroy the Bosnian Muslim group as such or a part thereof or, rather, to engage in ethnic cleansing during which period certain men were killed; we say because they were military-age men, not as part of the Bosnian Muslim group as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk, I thank you very much for your answer, and I have profited enormously from your contribution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm still a little -- if I might, Judge Meron, I have a nagging feeling that I never quite adequately answered Judge Schomburg's question this morning. Your Honour, if there's anything -- I'm particularly speaking about the strict construction. I, of course, tried to make that point throughout. And I know of no -- nothing that has derogated from that. If that was -- I realised after I gave my answer that I never really answered the first part of your question. And to my knowledge, I don't think that -- I know of no authority which has derogated from a strict construction of the 1948 Genocide Statute and certainly nothing that supports Professor Bassiouni's idea that this is a pliable definition to cover the kind of situations he was speaking of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: If I may just for a moment return to the last exchange you had with my learned colleague Judge Shahabuddeen. You seem now to be accepting that if all men of military age in Srebrenica were killed, and this would be equivalent to all men of procreative age, that this would amount to the destruction of the Muslim population of Srebrenica, which is a part for the purposes of the Genocide Convention of the entire group of Bosnian Muslims of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: With great respect, Your Honour, I don't mean that at all. No, I -- I certainly didn't mean to give that answer. What I thought I was answering with respect to Judge Shahabuddeen's question is that if the Appeals Chamber would hold that the elimination of the group from Srebrenica -- that is, the men together with the women, children, and elderly -- did indeed constitute the destruction of a part of a group, I think that we would have difficulties. We'd still claim that you have to look even further at all the facts and circumstances to see if there was truly an intent to destroy a part of the Bosnian Muslim group as such. But we certainly don't think, Your Honour - we strongly feel to the contrary - that the killing of the 7500 Bosnian Muslim men of military age for the reasons I tried to express in our brief and over the last few days is certainly not indicative and certainly doesn't prove beyond a reasonable doubt an intent to destroy a part of the Bosnian Muslim group as such.
