utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: If it were the women who were killed, would you have taken the same position?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we would have taken the same position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that you still wanted to return now to Judge Schomburg's -- or you have --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I simply wanted to mention to Judge Schomburg, as I realised -- this is in the thinking -- you know, I always realise what I could have said and should have said, and I just happened to think about it at the end of the -- when I was going down, frankly, to have a cup of coffee, that I -- it's a very important point. I mean, it's the heart of what this case is all about and the difference between the two sides. At bottom, our argument is that, in terms of in dubio pro re, in terms of nullum crimen sine lege, in terms of the usual rules of statutory construction, that the 1948 Genocide Convention is what governs here; it must be strictly construed the Committee of Experts' notion of it's sufficiently pliable to be changed, that it's not a static definition. We don't think that's so. We argue against that. And we think that in this situation a strict construction of the Genocide Statute as indicated not only by the Statute itself but by that long history. And the commentaries that I spoke about yesterday and today clearly indicate the -- and support the position we're taking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. If there are no further questions from my distinguished colleagues, we will now move on to the Prosecution and to its response. I take it, Mr. Farrell, you will start?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If you don't mind if I just ask Mr. Petrusic kindly if I could take the podium or remove the podium and transport it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So we will, at this stage, Mr. Farrell, go on until 1.00 p.m., and you will, also, continue later.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Please excuse me, Judge Schomburg; I'll try and be in a position where I can direct my attention towards you without the pole in the way. Just as a preliminary -- excuse me, a preliminary matter, there were a number of grounds of appeal that were not argued this morning, and we will direct our response to those that were argued. The ones that came up throughout the course of yesterday and today related to genocide, the intent for genocide, indirectly a parallel chain of command and the effect of the testimony, the additional evidence, on the Branjevo Farm, the intercept of July 16th. I will commence my submissions on the issue of genocide, and then my colleague, Ms. Karagiannakis, will proceed with the factual arguments. As you're aware, the Trial Chamber found after careful consideration of the facts that a genocide took place over approximately seven to nine days in July 1995 in the United Nations safe area. The essence of the Defence submissions on genocide is that the acts of the perpetrators, including General Krstic, can be no more than a criminal enterprise to forcibly displace the Bosnian Muslims at Srebrenica. As you're aware, the facts do not reflect this. The Trial Chamber was placed in a position where it had to ask itself a number of questions, including: Was it necessary for a displacement that you design a military operation based on a directive from the Supreme Commander that was to create an unbearable situation with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants? Was it necessary for the displacement of a group to execute the 7 to 8 thousand men and transfer the remaining? Was it necessary to hunt down all the Muslim men through -- from all four corners of the safe area and execute them, to destroy the homes of those after they have left and to destroy the mosques? The forced displacements, as characterised by the appellant, was initiated by an order of the Supreme Commander of the armed forces, Mr. Karadzic. This order arose on the 9th of July. And as we are aware, this order was sent directly to General Krstic. This order originated from the longstanding directive, which I've just referred to, which was to create a situation for no further survival or life. Approximately the same day, on July 9th, that the order was sent to General Krstic, who was in charge of the operation, the Supreme Commander told the civilian leader who was to become the civilian commissioner in Srebrenica that all those in Srebrenica must be killed. In fact, he said, "You need to kill everyone you can." Within approximately three days of this statement, the first of the 7 to 8 thousand Muslim men were executed. Within seven days, most of the killing was undertaken or completed. Within those seven days, President Karadzic deployed a police unit from Sarajevo to the Srebrenica area, Mr. Borovcanin, who arrived on July 11th and was instructed to contact General Krstic upon his arrival. General Krstic also had Colonel Beara attend in Bratunac to take care of detained prisoners by having them removed and killed. As well, Karadzic gave -- I'm sorry, Karadzic gave Beara the instructions. Plus, President Karadzic gave instructions regarding the meeting at the Hotel Fontana as a smokescreen. During the operation, it's the Prosecution's submission, and the Trial Chamber found that, General Krstic was intricately involved in the operation, both in the attack, in the bussing, and in supplying assets for the executions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Thank you. All the crimes were submitted within his zone of responsibility, and the Trial Chamber found that he shared the genocidal intent. He participated and contributed to the JCE. These acts, which have been characterised by the appellant as displacement, demonstrate a far more heinous crime: A hatred far greater than simply having people displaced. What happened in Srebrenica did not bear the same characteristics or follow the same methodology of the other historical examples that have been referred to you today. And it did not follow the same methodology of the examples we think of when we think of genocide, the Holocaust, or the situation in Rwanda. But the Holocaust and the Rwandan genocide should be considered cases of total genocide; in other words, where the objective of the perpetrators appeared to destroy the group in its entirety. In Krstic, what you, the Appeals Chamber, is faced with is being asked to consider the question of how to identify an intention to destroy a part of a group, and how does that intention manifest itself in reality? The inclusion of the concept of destruction in part in the Genocide Convention extends the reach of the Convention itself to cases where the perpetrators do not intend to destroy the group as a whole. It would therefore be a mistake to start the inquiry into the meaning of this phrase with the assumption that it applies to the situations of the Holocaust or the genocide in Rwanda. The difficult issue faced by the Trial Chamber was how to retain the essence of the Genocide Convention but at the same time give the plain meaning to the words that a perpetrator must simply intend to destroy a part. The appellant has raised in his oral submissions essentially four arguments: The first relates to the intent to commit genocide, especially due to the limited number of the persons killed, that being the men; and the fact that the women, children, and elderly were spared. The second submission is that the Trial Chamber's findings were consistent with displacement and not destruction, and as displacement is not one of the five enumerated acted for the commission of the crimes, the actus reus, it's not genocide. Thirdly, he made comments on the additional evidence. And fourthly, he tied up his arguments with attempting to make a submission on what constitutes a substantial part, and arguing that substantial part must be numerical and cannot be qualitative. I note that the last argument, the one that Mr. Sepenuk spent some time on yesterday and this morning, the last argument regarding the significant section of the group, the one related to the qualitative characteristics of the leadership; this is the first time that the Prosecution has heard this argument. It was not in the Notice of Appeal. It was not in the appeal brief. It was not mentioned in the reply brief. And therefore, I will attempt to respond to this ground of appeal, but I'm certainly - and I apologise - but I'm certainly in no position to determine whether or not there is any other material besides the material before this Court in the book of authorities which would assist you in determining whether or not this significant part -- if you accept the appellant's submission, whether the significant part is something that was referred to or is consistent with the objective of the Convention and the preparatory works. The first two grounds of appeal are similar in nature. For the most part, it's a -- with the exception of one aspect of it, it's essentially a factual argument, that the Trial Chamber erred in concluding that there existed an intent to commit genocide, especially in light of the limited number, and that the Trial Chamber's findings were more properly characterised with displacement. It's the Prosecution's submission that these are errors of law, with the one exception I'll deal with, but certainly they've asked this Appeals Chamber to consider that the findings were unreasonable. Before responding, I'd note that there may be -- there may be a different interpretation of the judgement between the Prosecution and the Defence which may affect your assessment of the judgement and the grounds of appeal, of course. It's the Prosecution's submission that the Trial Chamber found that the -- part of the group - and it's been referred to already in paragraph 560 - was the Bosnian Muslims of Srebrenica and that the group were the Bosnian Muslims and that the method or the means, the technique found by the Trial Chamber was that the killing of all the men in Srebrenica led to the result of the annihilation of the group in Srebrenica itself, as a group as such. And that is the part -- that's the Prosecution's interpretation of the judgement. It's my understanding that the appellant's interpretation is that -- or if the appellant's interpretation was accepted, that the Trial Chamber only found that the part was the men and they consist of a part of a part of the group. It's the Prosecution's submission that that was not the construction of the judgement by the Trial Chamber. If it was not the construction and if the part of the group was the Bosnian Muslims of Srebrenica, and that was a reasonable finding, then the first argument that the Defence raised, which is that the men themselves do not constitute a substantial part, would not hold water. They couldn't argue that because of the fact that the Court found that the men were the -- were part of the group and therefore that's not substantial. If the Trial Chamber's decision is read as the Prosecution reads it, that their identification of the part of the group was the Bosnian Muslims of Srebrenica, then this doesn't -- this isn't the substantial part. And as well, the qualitative aspect argument - the last one, saying that the Trial Chamber relied on finding that the men were a significant section of the group and that constituted the part of the group - if that's the case, then his argument remains part of a part of a group. The Prosecution's submission is that if the Trial Chamber actually found that the part of the group that was intended to be destroyed was the Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica, then we don't have to assess whether the men themselves were the substantial part. That's the Bosnian Muslims of Srebrenica. That's the Prosecution's position on the -- on the judgement and the way it affects the grounds. But I will proceed to argue and respond to the appellant's grounds as were raised. One of the arguments raised was that the Trial Chamber diluted the numerical requirement by finding that the targeted group, the targeted part, was the men. Now, as we've submitted, the targeted group was the Muslims of Srebrenica. The means was killing the men. But even assuming that we start with their premise, I would like to first clarify the facts a little. We don't, as I'm sure you're fully aware for the intent, look at the number of men killed. We don't start with the premise that the intent was to kill 7.500 men and from there you draw the inference that they therefore intended to destroy that group of 7.500. We look at a number of circumstances to decide intent. And relevant to that is the fact that the intention was to destroy -- I'm sorry, to kill the Muslim military-age men, as the Court said - and I'll come to that in a minute - but the men -- it wasn't to kill 7.500. It was to kill them all. The reason they were -- the actual numbers ended up at around 7.000 to 8.000 was because, as we know, they were unsuccessful to block the column, Colonel Pandurevic's troops were no able to block them. We even have an interim report which was sent back where he indicated that he could not successfully block and if he didn't get reinforcements he would have to let them go through. Now, based on the rest of the evidence, if they were able to capture those -- those members of the column that broke through, there is no doubt that they would have been killed. So the intention is not limited to killing 7.500, the intention is to killing all the Bosnian Muslim men that they -- that were in Srebrenica. That's a different number. That's between 10 and 15 thousand. And if that's the case, then the question is: Staying with the Defence's argument that it's only the men, is 10 to 15 thousand, the intended result, a substantial part of the Bosnian Muslims as a whole? In my respectful submission, it may very well be. The definition of "substantial part," of course, remains something that has to be interpreted, both legally and then applied factually. There are cases where there have been less. Nehemiah Robinson, one of the commentators, talks about a multiple of persons. The preparatory committee of the ICC understands the specific intention to be -- to destroy more than a small number of individuals. The Trial Chamber in Kayisheem and Rosandana says that is the intention to destroy is a considerable number of individuals. And the ultimate issue is if we accept that the part has to be substantial -- and I would indicate that there's nothing in the convention that says it has to be substantial; it simply says the word "part," and Judge Schomburg had asked if there'd been any change in the context of international customary law with respect to that issue. I'm not in a position - and I apologise - I'm not conversant enough to answer your question. I would just note that the Trial Chamber found that the commentators, Nehemiah Robinson and Drost, in 1949 and 1950 used words which were not substantial. Mr. Robinson made comments about substantial but characterised them in the context of "a multitude of persons." It's my understanding that the judgement itself recognises that at some point in time a stricter definition was used, and that was in the IL -- the International Law Commission report, and we accept for the sake of the judgement that that's the -- the number that the Trial Chamber worked from, which is the substantial part. But the interesting question for this Court is: Is substantial part relative, or is it in some way absolute? Does it have to be relative to the group? In other words -- Mr. Sepenuk said, it's point 0.5 per cent; therefore, it's not substantial. Does substantial have to be relative to the group at a whole or does it have to be a substantial in terms of its quantitative or numerical? It's the Prosecution's submission that -- excuse me. It's the Prosecution's submission that it would have to be the latter. It couldn't be that you killed a million people with genocidal intent in a country of 3 billion and were found not to have had the intent to destroy the group in part because the part was not substantial in relative terms. In this case, it's respectfully submitted, that though the Trial Chamber found that the part was the Bosnian Muslims of Srebrenica - and the Prosecution remains with that point - it could have found that the intent to kill upwards of 15.000 people substantial. The next Defence argument relates to the women, children, and the elderly and attempts to draw the inference that it would have been an unreasonable finding to conclude an intent to destroy the group when the women, elderly, and children were spared. There's one -- one preliminary issue I'd like to deal with in relation to their submissions, and that's their somewhat indulgent reliance on Professor Schabas's article in the Fordham International Law Journal. In his argument relating to the women and children, he refers to it three times. They were related to the possibility of other plausibility explanations, why someone would go to the trouble of evacuating the group, and I can't recall the third one, but I noted three times down. It's respectfully submitted that Professor Schabas, as a professor of law, passing judgement on what are plausible, factual conclusions, is of little assistance to this Court. In fact, all they do is mirror the submissions of the appellant. And the fact that they mirror them may support him in his article, but it's certainly not something that, in my submission, would be a matter of legal import that would assist this court in that determination. Professor Schabas may consider himself a judge after the article, but Professor Schabas can of course draw whatever instance he wants from the argument, but as he was not sitting in the court, does not know the evidence, did not hear it, and did not see it, what he thinks are other plausible explanations remain something for the classroom. In relation to the actual factual issue of not killing the women and children, we've made our submissions in the brief. I'm not going to go over that. What I would like to address is the relevance of the additional evidence. My colleague will address the additional evidence in more detail as it relates to the appellant, General Krstic. But just -- there's just a few interesting points in relation to the women and children. I've already referred to evidence on the trial record of Directive 7, which in the Prosecution's submission is somewhat indicative of President Karadzic's intention and instructions for the safe area. The witness Deronjic testified that President Karadzic's words to him were "Kill the Muslims, all those who were there, all those you can get your hands on." And he did that -- "Kill all those you can get your hands on," -- my recollection is he did that in the context of a question by Deronjic as to what to do with the civilians. Now, President Karadzic then says, "Well, it will be -- depend on the circumstances." And in the Prosecution's submission, the circumstances include the awareness and visibility of any crimes to the international community. At the end of the Directive 7 -- excuse me for one minute. Thank you. I just wanted to get the -- at the end of Directive 7, which is referred to in paragraph 28 of the judgement, you have a comment indicating what the objectives are that blocking aid convoys was part of the plan and indicating that they will reduce the allowance of the aid convoys but at the same time let them in in a limited way. The end of the directive from Karadzic says "Making them dependent on our good will while at the same time avoiding condemnation by the international community and the -- and international public opinion." Likewise, you'll see that when the decision is being made with respect to the civilians, it's the Prosecution's submission, and how to implement the statement by President Karadzic, the civilians that are in Srebrenica are encouraged by the UN Battalion in Srebrenica to go to Potocari. That's a finding by the Trial Chamber. In Potocari, they sought protection within the UN compound. There were UN soldiers. There were United Nations mission observers, UNMOs; there was the UN commander, and there was the UN deputy commander in Potocari. There were negotiations with the UN about the civilians on the 12th of July -- well, starting on the 11th in the evening and then on the 12th at the Hotel Fontana. And on the 12th of July the trial record indicate that is the Dutch Battalion was dealing with Kosoric and Nikolic, both subordinates of General Krstic, regarding the evacuation. Mr. Deronjic also spoke about when he discussed this matter with Karadzic - this matter being the men in Bratunac - he also indicated that they had to be moved -- moved to be killed because of the international community. Deronjic knew full well that when Beara came he was coming for a purpose that was discussed, in the Prosecution's submission, from Karadzic and for the purpose of killing. And what is Deronjic concerned about? He's concerned that they don't do it in his own back yard. Why? Because he says the international community is right there. When there are the negotiations on the 12th, what does Karadzic say to Deronjic? Mr. Deronjic is told basically, "Tell them three options. It's a smokescreen." There's one other matter which he's told, which is actually more telling. He's told to say that the men have to be separated because they're permitted under the laws of war to separate them, to screen them, as war criminals. What does Mladic say at the 12th of July Fontana meeting? He tells the members at the meeting - and this is found by the Trial Chamber - that the men are to be separated because they have to be screened for the purpose of war criminals. Karadzic tells Deronjic; Mladic says the exact same words. There's a coexistence between the two of them and the policy that is used to ensure that the men do not get on the buses. There's a justification that can be used as to why the men not be put on the buses, as they claim under the laws of war, and there's only a limited number; there's between 600 to 900 in Potocari, compared to the 20 to 25 thousand women, elderly, and civilians. Quite frankly, the only inference that it's much easier to do away with men than it is with the women. It's the same when the men are captured out on the road. The UN is a -- on the first transportation of the women and children to be forcibly expelled, the first one or two the UN has permitted to go. Then they're stopped. In fact, there's a finding in the judgement that 19 of the UN's vehicles are stopped as they try to take the buses of women and children and -- and go with them to sort of -- to the front line. Now, you must realise, of course, that the road that they're taking the women and children down on the 12th and the 13th is the road where the men are being captured. It's the Konjevic Polje-Bratunac road and it's the area where the capturing is going on by a number of the units. Now, the inference is that, in the Prosecution's submission, they're prevented from going because they will see what is happening to the men. When you add up those circumstances, it's not that the women were spared. Keep in mind that it wasn't as humanitarian as my learned colleague may try to make you believe. All the women and children and elderly were removed from the buses and forced to walk across the front line of up to a couple kilometres and were not bussed safely to the Muslim side. What you're left with, in the Prosecution's respectful submission, is a coherent and rational explanation consistent with the instructions by Karadzic as to why there is a difference in the treatment of the women, elderly, and the men. Just one last comment. I found it interesting that the justification that the screening of men was necessary for war crimes was not so far from the position of the Defence at trial regarding the killing of the men. The Defence military expert, General Radinovic, says - and I quote - "Mass casualties on the Muslim side are a result of actions which should be classified as combat activities." I think the findings of the Trial Chamber indicate how ridiculous this expert opinion is on that point. And once again, it's an attempt to justify the action in relation to the men, which can be done; it couldn't have been done in relation to the women. The Trial Chamber was fully apprised of the fact that the women, children, and elderly were not killed. This is not something new to them that may cause them to change their decision. And on the basis of the new evidence and the record of the evidence at trial, the Trial Chamber would clearly have come to no other decision. The Trial Chamber found at paragraph 595 that the killings and forcible transfer would have inevitably resulted in the physical disappearance of the Bosnian Muslim population. This is the physical disappearance of the Bosnian Muslims at Srebrenica. It is the physical disappearance of that part of the group which has been identified. And those -- some of the individuals, that being the women and children, the part of the group is not -- and without attempting to look like I'm adopting your questions, President Meron -- the Prosecution's position is that that part cannot reconstitute itself because of the fact that all the men were killed. If you remove all the men, you essentially remove the part of reproduction of that part. That group cannot reconstitute itself. In my submission, the argument of the appellant yesterday, relying on Professor Schabas's article that it would have been more logical to kill the women and children to complete the genocide act, has very little bearing when you're talking about the part. If you -- if you could -- and though I recognise that in my submission Mr. Sepenuk resiled from his earlier position and took the view that it wouldn't matter if the women and children were killed, my understanding of his submissions yesterday was if the women and children were killed, as referred to in the article by Professor Schabas, that would have been a different matter. The logic is the same. The logic is that without the ability to reproduce, that part would inevitably be destroyed. I will leave the third argument that was raised by the appellant regarding the linkages of the new evidence to General Krstic, though I may make some comments about it, but I think you'll hear that the Prosecution's position is that there is a very substantial link, if I can summarise it without taking away from my -- my colleague's submissions. There is a substantial link between the acts of the Supreme Commander, Mr. Karadzic, and the acts of the armed forces. It is not a separate split -- a separation or a split where General Krstic would have no idea what the operational side of Mr. Karadzic was doing. If you look at the evidence, the evidence is that the operational plan was assigned to the chief of staff for Krivaja '95; that's General Krstic. If you look at the evidence, Mr. Karadzic indicates that is he was working with Mr. Krstic -- with General Krstic in the planning of that operation. The evidence is that Deronjic says that they're concerned about Zivanovic, but he's not doing anything about the Muslims in Srebrenica, the ones that are escaping out and doing attacks out of the enclave, and Mr. Karadzic says, "Don't worry. I'll take care of it." In May, Karadzic says to Deronjic, "It's going to happen," as was asked in the question, "Your wish was granted." That's in May. That's a long time before the operation takes place and the July 2nd order takes place, but it's at the time when operations start. It's at the time when -- the takeover of the UN base Echo, at the end of May, and it's shortly after the attack on the 26th of June. In addition, on the 9th, when Deronjic speaks to Karadzic, he says, "I don't think the men that are down in Srebrenica are up to the task." He says, "I think you have to bring back Borovcanin. He's with the MUP, and I know him." That was on the 9th, the 8th or the 9th. On the 10th there is an order that Borovcanin leave the Sarajevo area and be in Srebrenica the next day by 12.00 noon and that he contact General Krstic. This is a link from Deronjic to Karadzic. Karadzic issues the order himself. The military unit from Sarajevo leaves and goes to Srebrenica, and who does he contact? Who is he ordered to contact when he arrives? General Krstic. When Deronjic has a problem, as I've indicated, about Zivanovic, he raises it with Karadzic and does Karadzic implement it as the military commander? Yes. And who was appointed? General Krstic. When Deronjic has a problem with the men in Bratunac, the captured men and doesn't know what to do with them as the civilian head, he contacts Karadzic. What happens? Within three to four hours a colonel arrives unannounced in his office to speak to him about what to do with the captured men. There is a clear link between Karadzic, the military operations, the killing of the men, the initial statement that they must be killed, and the role that Krstic played. And I'll leave that for my colleague to flesh out. The last submission I'll make - and I hope I can finish at least my part of the submissions by 1.00. It will only take me another five minutes or ten minutes to go through this - relates to the qualitative test, the significant section, that aspect that my learned colleague said was not part of international customary law and that the acceptance in a number of the decisions of the Trial Chamber that substantial part can have two components: A numerical component or a significant-section component. If I understand my colleague's submissions, he said the significant section part is not permissible and that notion is not found anywhere until 1985, in the special rapporteur, Mr. Whitaker's, report on genocide. Excuse me. As I've indicated, I unfortunately have not had the chance - though I'm tempted to look through some of the material last night to see whether or not there was anything to the argument that the preparatory works limited a substantial part to something that would exclude a significant section - I'm not in a position to -- to assist. And if the Court feels that it would be assistance, of course we will do some research and file something, as this wasn't raised in the appeal brief. So we haven't addressed it. But just let me speak to the issue, if I may. If you think through what the objective of the Convention is, the objective is essentially to protect a group or a part and to protect it from destruction. Those are, as far as I could think of, the two distinguishing factors. Acts which do either -- that destroy either -- intend to destroy either the whole or the part are criminalised. It's clearly the physical or biological destruction, and it's not cultural, and the Trial Chamber specifically found that at paragraph 580. All the material that my learned colleague went through to say that the cultural aspects of members of a community are not protected per se under the Convention, and specifically his reference to the ad hoc committee's draft, relate only to the aspects of their cultural existence. I'll just read a passage from the ad hoc committee's draft. It's not necessary for you -- I'll simply indicate where it is, if you care to refer to it. At registry page 4696 of the appellant's additional materials, this draft states: "Means of cultural genocide and subsection B: Forced and systematic exile of individuals representing the culture of the group." It lists the members, scholars, writers, artists, teachers, so on. And it says: "The cultured and moral -- the cultural and moral life of a group is sustained by its cultured members. If these are removed, the group is no more than an amorphous and defenceless mass. Its language is degraded. It's reduced to a position of inferiority, and the language itself has no longer any political or social significance." This is not what we're talking about in the Whitaker report and what the -- in my respectful submission, the Trial Chambers have found is a significant section. We're not talking about protecting the cultured members. We're not talking about their exile. We're not talking about degrading their language so they have no political or social significance. That's not what this is. That's not what the use of significant section refers to. And the reliance on this passage, though close in language, is far in terms of its intent. What, in my submission, the leadership characteristics of a significant section are relevant to is the ultimate survival of the group. And that's the very object and purpose of the convention. The question is: How do you interpret the word "significant part" or "significant section"? Is is it consistent with the purpose of and object of the Genocide Convention? It's my submission that it certainly is, and in fact it's equally consistent with the use in the Jelisic Trial Chamber. The issue is whether or not a substantial part has been identified for the purposes of a part of a group. It's clear that it appears that the passages referred to by my learned colleague refer to its numerical size. The question is: If a significant section of the group will result or call into question the very survival of the group, why would it not be considered if it's not a large number? The substantial part is a numerical or quantitative criterion. But if the object and purpose of the Convention is the destruction of the group, if a smaller number not classified as numerically substantial, but a smaller number has the same effect, then why would the Convention not protect them if the effect is for the purpose of destroying the group? In fact, it's -- in a way it's somewhat ironic, the argument that's made by my learned colleague. If you can think of a hypothetical where the head is cut off and the body does not survive, the whole group is gone. And if the head is the significant part or the significant section, you actually may have a destruction of a group, a group of indigenous people that require or rely on a particular section for their survival. Once you kill, or destroy, or get rid of that group that has significance to the survival of the indigenous population, you could draw the inference that the intention was to destroy the group. Now, that's a smaller number than a substantial part. If you went into that indigenous group and you actually killed a substantial part numerically, you will succeed with finding that genocide occurred, even though the group may continue to exist. While in the other instance, where the group doesn't exist, it wouldn't be genocide, because all you killed was a numerically smaller part but it happened to have some significance. That can't be the -- the end result of the application of this -- this criteria. It has to be that as long as the destruction is with the intent to destroy, and the group, the part may be smaller, but if it has some effect on the larger group, then the result would be the same. Those are all the submissions I can make on that -- that issue, unless -- well, it's close to the end, and I don't know if at this point in time you'd like to take the break before I pass it over to Mrs. Karagiannakis -- Ms. Karagiannakis, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Farrell. It is now 1.25. And, of course, after the break, the -- the response by the Prosecution will continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: If my colleagues are agreeable, I would suggest that we pose our questions after the completion of the -- of the response by the Prosecution. So if it were convenient, I would suggest that we would now rise until 2.30 p.m. And I thank you for your argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. We will now continue with the response by the Prosecution. I believe that Mr. Farrell finished for the time being and that Ms. Karagiannakis will now take over. Ms. Karagiannakis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will be addressing factual issues for you today. The first factual issue I'll be addressing is the -- General Krstic's intent for genocide and how the facts establish that and how, therefore, the Trial Chamber judgement is correct. And then I will be addressing points made by learned counsel on issues of the involvement of the MUP, the alleged parallel chain of command, which Mr. Petrusic addressed, and finally the Branjevo Farm. Prior to commencing my submissions, I'd just like to make three points of clarification. Judge Shahabuddeen, you asked counsel for the Defence whether there was any evidence on the record that Karadzic knew about executions during the time that they were occurring. I'd like to direct Your Honour to transcript page numbers 124 and 125 and transcript page number 116 of Deronjic's testimony, where on three separate occasions he says that he advised Karadzic of mass executions, including the execution at the Kravica warehouse. The second point of clarification I'd like to make was - and I apologise to counsel if I misheard what they said - but I understood that counsel had answered the Judge -- one of the Judge's questions by saying that Karadzic said that the prisoners were to be sent to Batkovici. Well, that does not accord with transcript page number 117 and 120 of Deronjic's testimony. Karadzic didn't say that the men were going to be sent to Batkovici. What he -- this was Deronjic's supposition about what Karadzic meant. It's not what Karadzic said. And it's our submission, obviously, Your Honours, that you should rely on the direct -- the direct statements that are reported by Deronjic and said by Karadzic, as opposed to Deronjic's interpretation of what they may or may not mean. Finally, I understood Defence counsel to say to Your Honours that there was no evidence of any direct participation or knowledge of Mr. Krstic in the killing operation. I would refer, on the record -- I would refer Your Honours to the Trial Chamber judgement, paragraphs 378 to 423, where the evidence that they relied on to find knowledge and participation are referred to. With those matters clarified, Your Honours, I will move on to my submission in relation to intent for genocide. Actually, there is one other matter that I'd like to address before that. It was suggested by Your Honour that it was men of military age who were targeted. Now, I think it's important to clarify what it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: This was not suggested by me. This was in the decision of the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, when the Trial Chamber is referred to men of military age through its judgement, it actually clarifies what it means at footnote 3 of the judgement and I'd like just to read that out to you. The Trial Court said, "Throughout this judgement, the term 'military age' is used to describe the group of men who were captured and executed following the takeover of Srebrenica. It is a misnomer to the extent that some boys were --" I'm sorry, I can't read it. There's a stamp over it -- "where some men and some boys who were several years younger and several years older than -- than would generally be considered military age were included within this group. Consequently, the term should be understood in its broadest non-technical sense as including the men and boys who were broadly defined by the Bosnian Serb authorities as being within the vicinity of the military age." So it's not a strict definition that the Court was using, it's a generic one. Further, factual findings support that it wasn't the military group that was being targeted. It wasn't the defence forces. The VRS killed all of the men of procreative age; indeed, even more younger men and older men. For that proposition, I'd refer to -- I'd refer Your Honours to the exhibits at trial 276 and 274, which were demographic reports, and they concluded out of the 7.475 persons dead, 199 of them were under 17 years of age; 739 of them were above 60 years of age, and 48 are -- who are missing are actually women, and included in the missing group are two 8-year-old girls. Also relevant to this point is that most of the people that were killed were civilians. The column was 10.000 to 15.000 people large. One-third was the 28th Division; that is, the military group. They broke through and escaped, leaving the majority of civilian men to be captured. And I refer Your Honours to the Trial Chamber findings at paragraph 60 to 65 on this issue. In addition, many of the people who were killed were -- and were found in the graves were severely handicapped, deformed, or ill. They were civilians physically unable to contribute to the Muslim war effort. Finally, the Trial Chamber held that the decision to execute the men was unfathomable in military terms. I refer Your Honours to the Trial Chamber findings at paragraph 70. So when reference is made to military men, Your Honours, it's not referring to an army. It's referring to basically everyone -- all the men they could get their hands on. Having addressed that general point, I'd like to move on to the issue of the evidence that establishes Krstic's genocidal intent. And what I will try to do is refer Your Honours to the trial judgement and also the additional evidence and how that may affect your decision-making process. My learned leader, Mr. Farrell, has already addressed Radovan Karadzic's strategic goals for the enclave. The Defence on Friday used the term "invisible" to describe General Krstic. Today I think they used the word "passive." It is the Prosecution's submission that General Krstic was not the invisible man; he was the indispensable man to this murder operation. General Krstic was appointed as a result of Karadzic's wish to replace Zivanovic. And for that proposition I refer you to Deronjic's transcript 158 to 159. When Karadzic was considering Plan B, i.e., to take the enclave on the 8th and 9th, who did he send his order to personally? General Krstic. General Krstic admitted during the trial, at transcript page references 2163 to 2165, that he was familiar with Karadzic's Directive 1 and he was also familiar with the subsequent order from the Main Staff, 7.1, and that's General Mladic, which resulted in him drawing up the plan for Krivaja '95. He was Karadzic's man. General Krstic took a lead role in the military operation. As of the 6th of July, 1995, he led the attack on Srebrenica from the Drina Corps forward command post at Pribicevac, which was at an elevation looking down on the town of Srebrenica. He commanded that operation at least until the arrival of General Mladic on the 9th of July. The Trial Chamber found that basically the Bosnian Serbs had succeeded. They had met very little resistance and succeeded in the operation to shrink the enclave and this resulted in a subsequent action to try and take the enclave. Again, they didn't meet much resistance. On the basis of this fact and other facts, the Trial Chamber found that the VRS forces shelled Srebrenica town on the 10th and the 11th of July in order to terrorise the population and drive them out of Srebrenica towards Potocari; i.e., this was the beginning of the forcible expulsion. I'd like to read out the judgement, paragraph 337, about General Krstic's role in this. "The Trial Chamber finds that General Krstic was well aware of the shelling of Srebrenica, would drive tens of thousands of Bosnian Muslim civilians from the town into the small area of Potocari they thought safe because of the UN base there. He must have known, inevitably, basic needs for shelter, food, water, and medicine at the site would prove overwhelming. The Trial Chamber further finds that General Krstic was fully appraised of the VRS territorial goals in the Srebrenica enclave, which included cleansing the area of the Bosnian Muslim population." So General Krstic was at the very least, on the basis of what the Trial Chamber found, deliberately participating as a senior officer in Pribicevac, trying to drive out the population from the 11th. That is very far from the proposition put by the Defence that he was a humanitarian seeking to protect the civilian population. Your Honour, much is made by the Defence about findings relating to planning of the operation. What we can see from the directive and the incremental increases -- incremental increase in the attacks on Srebrenica, from starving the enclave all the way to Krivaja '95, all the way to Karadzic ordering that it be taken, was that the Bosnian Serbs had one strategic goal in mind. But were reacting to the situation on the ground and were formulating operational plans as and when they understood what was going to happen. This is where the first piece of very critical additional evidence comes in. At the trial, this evidence wasn't available. We didn't know when precisely the plan -- the operational plan, as opposed to the strategic goal -- had been made in relation to the takeover of Srebrenica. Well, Mr. Nikolic has now told us in his testimony when at least he knew of the plan. In his evidence, he said that sometime prior to the third Hotel Fontana meeting at 10.00 in the morning he met with Lieutenant Colonel Popovic, a security officer from the Drina Corps; and Lieutenant Colonel Kosoric; he is not a security officer. He also happens to be the brother-in-law of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] What date was that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: This is the 12th of July, Your Honour. And they -- he asked them, what's going to happen to all these people? Actually, I will quote. And it's transcript page number 1676. "Q. What if anything was said between you, Lieutenant Colonel Popovic and Kosoric that morning in the hotel? Nikolic answers: "A. Yes, we talked. And in answer to my question to Popovic and Kosoric as to what would happen next, Lieutenant Colonel Popovic told me on that day that women and children would be evacuated and they would -- and they would be evacuated in the direction of Kladanj. Also on that day, the men, the able-bodied men, would be separated and those men would be temporarily detained once they had been separated. And when I asked what would happen to them next, he told me that all the balijas needed to be killed." Here we have an eyewitness account that we didn't have at trial and the Trial Chamber didn't have available to it of the earliest date at which we can put a firm -- a firm operation to kill. And what is this operation? It isn't -- there is no separation here between transportation and killing. It's all part of one plan: The women and children will be shipped out and the men will be killed. Now, how does this affect the Trial Chamber findings, particularly in relation to General Krstic's intent? That's the critical issue. Let me put this in context for Your Honours. The night before, Krstic had attended the Fontana meeting. Nikolic, on the following morning, at about 8.00 sees Mladic, Krstic, Popovic and Kosoric at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters. At this time we also know that Mladic, Krstic, and Vasic meet for the purposes of assigning tasks, and we know that from the Annex 3 to the Prosecution Further Notice. At this time it is also found by the Trial Chamber that the VRS know that the column is trying to get out of Srebrenica. Then, before the meeting, Popovic and Kosoric tell Nikolic what the plan is. Immediately afterwards, Mladic goes into the third and final Hotel Fontana meeting with Krstic and he tells the representatives there that the men have to be screened. Now, when he is saying that, in light of this evidence, Your Honour, he knows they're not going to be screened; this is his excuse to separate the men out so that he can begin his killing operation. Subsequently, General Krstic, who's also of course at the meeting, engages in organising the buses. Later that day Krstic was present in Potocari for 1 and a half hours. He was aware of the separations and the horrible conditions there. Also in Potocari were Popovic, Kosoric, and Nikolic. And he -- I refer Your Honours to transcript 1694 to 95. If Krstic didn't know what the plan was, he must Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. have been the only one who didn't in these circumstances. He is seen with all of the key players in this planning operation on the day. He meets with them. He assigns tasks. He's with Mladic. He then takes on the organisation of one part of the genocidal plan, which is to transport the women and children out of the enclave. Your Honours, if Your Honours accept this evidence and the only conclusion available from this evidence and the other matters I have mentioned, then that means that General Krstic's participation from that moment on, every way that he -- everything that he does in order to further the plan of transportation and executions is knowing and intentional and is an act in pursuance of a genocidal JCE. After the Hotel Fontana meeting, after the plan has been hatched, General Krstic goes on -- General Krstic goes on to be a critical player in the organisation of the -- of the transport of the Bosnian Muslim women and children. He personally directed a complicated logistics phase essential for the accomplishment of the overall criminal purpose. Further, the buses that General Krstic knowingly arranged to send the women and children out of the enclave were the same buses that were diverted to take separated and captured men from detention locations in Bratunac from the 12th and the 13th of July, and I refer the Court to the judgement 157 to 161. He was responsible for securing the route out of the enclave, and he must have known that men were being separated out at Tisca and taken to detention sites. Now, in light of the new evidence, he must have also been known that these people were going to be killed. I refer Your Honours to Trial Chamber paragraphs 368 to 369. Krstic's buses were then used to take prisoners from Bratunac to Zvornik for mass executions on the 13th. I refer Your Honours to 179 to 186 of the judgement. There's also a specific finding that the buses organised by Krstic were diverted in order to pick men up from the collection points along the Konjevic Polje road and taken to the Kravica warehouse where they died -- where they were killed. Also, there is a finding by the Trial Chamber in relation to the Branjevo Farm massacre. Mr. Erdemovic recognises the marks on some of the buses, and the Trial Chamber finds in that regard that these are buses that were previously used to transport women and children out but were now being used to take people to their death at the Branjevo Farm. All of these acts are acts of participation in the overall joint plan to kill and expel. The transportation of the women and children was completed at approximately 8.00 p.m. on the 13th of July; early evening, late evening. This was a critical point in the operation, Your Honour -- or in the plan. Up until that point, the men had been separated in Potocari, the women and children had been shipped out, and there'd been one mass execution at the Kravica warehouse. What remained to be done? What remained to be done in this case was the murder of the rest of the 7 and a half thousand people. Five hundred people were killed at the Kravica warehouse. So this was a very critical point in this joint plan. What happened at that point? At that point, General Krstic was appointed as commander of the Drina Corps by General Mladic. And this is not just a passive process. He assumed command of the Drina Corps. We know this because an eyewitness told the Trial Chamber - Witness II - that he was at the ceremony as the Vlasenica Brigade headquarters at -- between 4.00 and 6.00 in the afternoon and that General Mladic appointed General Krstic as the head of the Drina Corps. Subsequently President Karadzic as commander-in-chief issued a decree that he would become the commander. What does this tell us? The only logical -- the only inference that can be drawn from this is that Mladic and Karadzic knew and had confidence in General Krstic. They knew that he would fulfil the tasks that were -- that were assigned to the Drina Corps. What were those tasks? Those tasks were combat operations, capturing prisoners, killing prisoners, and the attack on Zepa. His appointment and assumption of command is -- is in itself an active participation in this plan. He is accepting the responsibility to ensure that he and his subordinate units in the Drina Corps actually fulfil all the tasks that have been assigned to them by their superior command. At this point I'd like to refer Your Honours to some additional evidence that we have. Annex 7, Annex 11, and Annex 14 of the Prosecution's rebuttal evidence. In relation in general to the Prosecution's rebuttal evidence, the Prosecution refers the Chamber to its written submissions contained in the Prosecution's confidential notice and filing of rebuttal evidence and arguments in compliance with the Appeals Chamber scheduling order of 3rd October 2003. I won't go into detail; I just want to make a couple of points. Each of the three documents that I've referred to are combat reports from General Krstic and signed by or for him, sent as commander of the Drina Corps to the Main Staff. Annex 7 is the earliest report where you see General Krstic's signature block as the commander of the Drina Corps. It's received by the communications centre at 19.45, which corroborates the evidence that he was in fact the commander at this point. This is consistent with the Trial Chamber's findings at paragraph 331 of the judgement. Annex 11 and 14 are issued on the 16th and the 18th of July, respectively. In the 13 and 16 July reports, General Krstic evidences a detailed knowledge about what all the Drina Corps subordinate brigades are doing in the whole area of responsibility, including Zepa, Srebrenica, and Zvornik. And he also takes decisions about what they're going to do in the future, and he tells the Main Staff what those decisions are going to be. In both of these reports --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Excuse me. The date of the report mentioned in Annex 7?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: The date of that report is the 13th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: In both of these reports, General Krstic decides that his troops are to coordinate with the MUP in blocking and capturing Bosnian Muslims escaping from the enclave. This directly refutes the proposition put by learned counsel that in fact the MUP was acting completely on its own in this operation. General Krstic's own documents issued as the commander of the Drina Corps firmly rebut those submissions. The important thing about these reports is that they span the main execution period in the Zvornik Brigade from the 14th of July -- 14th to the 17th of July and therefore provide incontrovertible evidence that General Krstic was in effective command and control of all the Drina Corps units in the area of responsibility of the corps. Your Honours, command is not an optional activity. It's a position of control and responsibility and leadership. General Krstic was the commander of the Drina Corps. He was therefore responsible under military doctrine for everything his subordinate units did. The Trial Chamber recognised the strict nature of control exercised by commander at paragraph 268 of the judgement in the course of its reasoning where it totally rejects the arguments -- the various arguments put forth by the Defence for parallel chain of command. The only inference that can be drawn pursuant to this principle, pursuant to the additional evidence and the evidence referred to by the Trial Chamber in the paragraphs I've previously mentioned to you, is that from the time General Krstic assumed command of the Drina Corps on the evening of the 13th of July, his troops, including those at the lowest levels, were acting in accordance with his wishes and were reporting back to him. He, in turn, was acting in accordance with the wishes of his superiors - in this case, General Mladic, commander of the VRS, and ultimately Radovan Karadzic, commander of -- Supreme Commander. General Krstic's participation doesn't stop there, Your Honours. Witness II reported that General Krstic drove down the Konjevic Polje road on the 13th of July. That same evening General Krstic has a conversation with the MUP commander, Borovcanin. The additional evidence that we have indicates that Borovcanin admitted to Deronjic that his men had carried out the Kravica mass execution. I refer Your Honours to Deronjic T-page -- transcript 124. This is also corroborated by the additional evidence of Dragan Obrenovic at transcript page 2527 to 2529. In that -- I'll read out that conversation to Your Honours: "Krstic: Hello, this is Krstic. "Borovcanin: Hello. This is Borovcanin. General, how are you? "Krstic, "Well, where are you, fuckers? "Borovcanin: I'm here at the command post. "Krstic: How's it going? "Borovcanin: It's going well. Krstic: "Don't tell me you have any problems. "Borovcanin: "I don't, I don't." Borovcanin's troops had committed a mass execution that day and Borovcanin was reporting to Krstic and telling him that things were going well. Yet another piece of evidence that shows that he knew and agreed with wholeheartedly the murder operation and was indeed monitoring the MUP forces on the road, which, again, directly contradicts the submissions put by learned Defence. The next piece of critical participation: The trial -- now, I should just point out that it's true that General Krstic was indeed the commander of the Zepa operation at this time, but the Trial Chamber finds that he is constantly travelling the 34 kilometres between the Drina Corps forward command post in Vlasenica and the Zepa operation and that he's also in communication with all of the officers in his zone of responsibility. Now, when Krstic was at the Zepa operation, one of the main commanders that was with him was the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, Vinko Pandurevic. The Trial Chamber -- now, Vinko Pandurevic was down there not on his own, obviously, but with Zvornik Brigade units participating with General Krstic in the Zepa operation. The Trial Chamber found that Pandurevic was ordered back to Zvornik. The question, of course, was: Why? The finding was that Pandurevic was ordered back to his area of responsibility --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I think it would be useful if you were to slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Pardon me, Your Honour. The Trial Chamber found that Pandurevic was ordered back to his area of responsibility on the 14th of July, 1995, in light of the dual problems of Muslim combatants and prisoners. They found that General Krstic ordered him back. This is yet another piece of direct participation in the JCE. General Krstic knew that the Zvornik Brigade was having problems in dealing with combat and killing. What is his reaction? He sends the commander of the Zvornik Brigade and his units back to Zvornik. Admittedly, Pandurevic engaged in combat activities, but to facilitate the tasks of the Zvornik Brigade at that time. The findings in relation to this issue, Your Honour, can be -- are at paragraphs 399 and 474. Not only does the Trial Chamber make that finding. They find that once Pandurevic is back in the Zvornik Brigade area of responsibility he is reporting to General Krstic about all of the things that are going on in that zone of responsibility. That includes the murder of thousands of men between the 14th and the 17th and also the combat operations. In particular, I refer Your Honours to an important document relied upon by the Trial Chamber, that is, the 16 July combat report from Pandurevic to the Drina Corps command, where he expressly refers to the strain that the joint tasks of combat and prisoners is causing him. The next piece of direct participation: The Beara 15 July intercept. The Defence has made two submissions, if I understand correctly, in relation to this intercept. One of the submissions relates to what the intercept tells us about General Krstic's knowledge and intent, which was addressed by Mr. Sepenuk; and the other submission was whether or not any action followed from the intercept, which was addressed by Mr. Petrusic. For the purposes of this argument of participation, I'll just address knowledge and intent, and I will address the participation and follow-up of that intercept later in my submissions. Your Honours, if I may refer you to the intercept in the judgement which can be found at paragraph 380. And I'll make some submissions on it, and then I foreshadow using a diagrammatical aid to assist in my oral submissions. First of all, it's interesting to note that in relation to this intercept General Krstic denied ever having had that conversation at trial. This is referred to by the Trial Chamber at 385 of the judgement. He said he -- in fact, he never had any conversation with Colonel Beara between the 13th and the 17th of July. It appears as though, in their submissions, the Defence is now saying that indeed the conversation did occur but that the interpretation given to it by the Trial Chamber is not the correct one. In the Prosecution's submission, it is certainly the correct one, particularly in terms of intent and knowledge. It is not contested that in this conversation Beara is considering Krstic for manpower to kill 3 and a half thousand prisoners. What is Krstic's response? His response, very simply, is -- he says he'll see what he can do. And he doesn't just say it once or twice, but he says it three times throughout the intercept. "I'll see what I can do. I'll see what I can do. I'll see what I can do." He knows the murder operation is going on, and he's offering his assistance. Now, in order to better illustrate that point, Your Honours, I have a diagram or -- I'd like to refer to a diagram. Now, I had provided this diagram to the legal officer and the Defence this morning, and I just wanted to use this as an aid to my oral submissions in order to basically speed them up and make the points a little bit more quickly. This diagram is no more than a representation of the -- the structure of the Drina Corps, as found by the Trial Chamber. Oh, sorry, it's the first -- sorry. Pardon me, Your Honours. It's the first diagram. And I'd ask that you be permitted to view it. I understand my -- my colleague has something to say about it. But I'd ask that you be permitted to have a look at what it is so you can deal with the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: May I just inquire what is the view of the Defence about our viewing this?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is not customary that when arguments -- legal arguments are being presented, particularly in appeals, this kind of objection is made, but the Defence considers this to be evidence on the part of the Prosecution for the simple reason that my learned colleague is referring to an intercept which was transcribed and made note of and which exists as an exhibit and existed during the -- during the trial as an exhibit. So that looking at this diagram, which we were given this morning, I feel that it is a new piece of evidence and possibly it was the intention on the part of the Prosecution to use this diagram to show the participants in the conversation. But the participants in the conversation were represented in the Prosecution exhibits during the trial stage and the conversation held on the 15th of July, in actual fact, between General Krstic and Colonel Beara. So they were the sole, direct participants in that particular conversation. They were on the telephone line. So that I consider that this diagram, regardless of the shape and form it takes, whether as a new piece of evidence or whether it is termed in any other way, I do not consider that it can be relevant when interpretations are made of this particular intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrusic. I will consult with the Bench and we will give our ruling in a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Could I ask the Prosecution whether she really needs this diagram to introduce it now, whether she cannot make -- whether you cannot make your argument without referring to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Ms. Karagiannakis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Of course, as Your Honour pleases. Well, I'll simply make my submissions of the diagram containing the judgement, which is quite smaller and a little bit more difficult to see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I would really appreciate that. Out of fairness to the Defence, I would prefer not to include it at this very late stage. Just make -- I think you could make your argument without referring to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Yes. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So please carry on with your argument. I do appreciate your cooperation on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: I'd just like to go through the names mentioned in the intercept and point out who these people were -- are. The first person mentioned is Furtula. Beara says: "General" -- to Krstic -- "Furtula didn't carry out the boss's order." Your Honours, Furtula is the commander of the 5th Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade. This is a subordinate unit of Krstic. Beara says: "I need 30 men, like it was ordered." Krstic says to him: "Take them from Nastic or Blagojevic." Lieutenant Colonel Milomir Nastic is the commander of the 1st Milici Light Infantry Brigade. He is also a subordinate of General Krstic. Blagojevic is also -- he's the Bratunac Brigade commander; again, a subordinate of General Krstic. It goes on. Krstic says: "Again, check with Nastic. Check with Blagojevic." I.e., check with my subordinate commanders about getting these men. Then he says: "Check with Blagojevic and take his Red Berets." The Red Berets are a unit of the Bratunac Brigade; again, subordinates of General Krstic. Then Krstic says: "Take -- then take those MUP -- Ministry of the Interior guys from up there." Beara says: "No, they won't do anything. I talked to them. There's no solution for the men -- for those 15 to 30 men with Indic." So Beara is saying that the MUP is not going to do the executions. Then he suggests there's no solution for those 15 to 30 men with Indic. Who is Indic? Indic is a subordinate of Major Furtula, who I've just mentioned, and both of those men are actually subordinates of General Krstic at this time. Then General Krstic says: "Ljubo, you have to understand me. You guys fucked me up so much." And in the submission of the Defence this is some sort of evidence of reluctance, disapproval, some -- showing that he doesn't really want to help in this murder operation. Your Honours, I'd like to refer you to the specific consideration of the this reluctance by the Trial Chamber. The findings in this regard can be found at paragraph 382. It says: "General Krstic's initial reluctance to provide any men for Colonel Beara is consistent with the fact that by this time units of the Zvornik Brigade had been withdrawn from Zepa and sent back to address the urgent situation in their zone of responsibility." The reason that there is some type of reluctance is because he's -- General Krstic has already sent men away from Zepa back to Zvornik in order to meet the dual requirements of killing in combat and he just doesn't want to lose any more men. But he doesn't say no. He says, "I'll see what I can do. I'll see what I can do. I'll see what I can do," and he refers Beara to -- everybody he refers to -- everybody who is referred to in here is a subordinate of him. He refers Beara to all -- to a number of his subordinates. "Take the killers from my subordinates." That's what's going on here, Your Honour. So putting aside the issue of whether anybody actually arrived - which I will address later - this is incontrovertible knowledge of -- this is incontrovertible proof of General Krstic's knowledge of the murder operation and the fact that he is a willing participant in it, and frankly is one of the most important and critical pieces of evidence showing his genocidal intent. He is offering to help in this exercise. The final point I'd like to make in this regard, Your Honours, is the reason why Beara needs to talk to General Krstic. The Main Staff is an organisational shell. It only has two operational units: The 10th Sabotage Detachment and the 65th Protection Regiment. It doesn't have manpower. That's why Beara is forced to seek personnel to conduct this murder operation from the Drina Corps and indeed from the MUP, and is this case the MUP won't do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Do you -- can you explain why?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Well, I think it's apparent from the intercept. He's -- Ljubo, "I asked the MUP, but they won't do it."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Why wouldn't they do it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Why wouldn't they do it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't speculate as to why the MUP won't do it. But clearly Beara is saying the MUP won't do it here. So I can't take that any further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Although -- actually, when I think about it, this is the 15th of July, and what we do know from the additional evidence presented by the Defence is that Vasic -- that there are basically two MUP units operating in the Srebrenica operation. One of them is Borovcanin, who I've mentioned previously, and the other one is Vasic. Vasic is the person who's sending the reports to the MUP that are the -- additional evidence of the Defence. Now, in those reports, Vasic is talking about the difficulties that they're having -- the obligations that they have to capture men on the road and that they're having difficulties in dealing with it. So there may be an explanation in that; i.e., they don't have the manpower either. One thing is certainly true: In terms of manpower in that region, it's the Drina Corps that has thousands of soldiers there. As far as we know, the MUP forces there are constitute bid two groups, Borovcanin and Vasic, and that there are only two groups available to the Main Staff. For this reason, I think the Trial Chamber in fact makes a finding about this. And if you'll just give me a moment, I'll find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I'll do is during the break I will -- after I sit down, I'll try and -- I will ask my colleagues to try and find that reference. So as not to lose time, I will proceed. But there's a finding in the Trial Chamber judgement about the Drina Corps being indispensable to the -- to the conduct of this operation, along those lines that I've explained. Now I come to the final and perhaps the most compelling piece of evidence with respect to General Krstic's exercise of command in relation to the executions. It was General Krstic's submission or position at trial that Colonel Popovic was one of the key security officers who were -- who was running and monitoring the murder operation. He alleged that Popovic was operating pursuant to a parallel chain of command. The evidence presented at trial and the Trial Chamber's findings fairly firmly refute that position, as does the additional evidence, which I will go into later on in my submissions. But the Trial Chamber finds that Popovic -- who Krstic himself says was critical in organising and monitoring the murder operation -- actually reports back to General Krstic, and they find that this is evidence of General Krstic monitoring his subordinates in the killing operation. These findings can be found at paragraphs 400 to 404. Now, one of the intercepts relied on there is a subject of argument before Your Honours, and that's the 16th of July intercept. I intend to show Your Honours why the additional evidence in fact supports this finding and does not affect it at all. Popovic was reporting to Krstic. And I'd just like to make reference to -- quote one final intercept in relation to that. At 403 of the Trial Chamber judgement, it states: "Further intercepts taken on the 17th of July 1995 support a finding that Colonel Popovic was reporting to the Drina Corps command and specifically to General Krstic about executions. At 12.42 on that day, Zlatar 1, which is the code name associated with General Krstic as the Drina Corps commander, called Major Golic from the Drina Corps intelligence section looking for Colonel Popovic. Major Golic, referring to Zlatar 1 as General, informed him that Popovic is still in Zvornik but will be back in the afternoon. Zlatar 1, General Krstic, then instructed Mr. Golic to find Popovic and have him call the forward command post immediately. He's telling him, "Report to me immediately." Several hours later, Colonel Popovic was overheard in an intercepted conversation in which he said the following: "Hello, it's Popovic. Boss, everything is okay. That job is done. Everything is okay. Everything has been brought to an end. No problems. I'm at the base, at the base. That all gets an A, an A. The grade is an A. Everything is okay. That's it. Bye. Take care." The Trial Chamber states that, "Although General Krstic was not specifically identified in the conversation, given that the executions have been completed by this time, and the preceding conversation in which General Krstic was seeking a report from Popovic and Popovic's reference to "boss", the inference is very strong that this conversation recorded Colonel Popovic recording -- reporting to General Krstic about the completion of the executions." And not just that; about the A-job that the Drina Corps has done in the completion of the executions. There are a number of other pieces of evidence referred to in the trial judgement that go directly to General Krstic's participation. Corroborative evidence is found by the Trial Chamber in the sense that -- from paragraphs 406 through to 412, that he is in contact with the critical players in the murder operation. First and foremost General Krstic; Colonel Beara; Colonel Popovic; Colonel Pandurevic, commander of the Zvornik Brigade. Basically not only was there no parallel chain of command here, Your Honour, but General Krstic was in the centre and communicating with all the critical people engaged in this murder operation. His boss, General Mladic; his colleague, Colonel Beara; his subordinates, Colonel Popovic and Colonel Pandurevic. The inescapable conclusion, Your Honour, is that General Krstic was in on the expulsion and murder plan from the beginning and that he was constantly monitoring his troop's participation in it, which is detailed in the Trial Chamber findings and have -- has been addressed by my colleagues previously, but there's extensive Drina Corps participation in the murders. It is this evidence that was relied upon by the Trial Chamber to find him guilty of genocide and their findings were entirely reasonable, particularly in respect of the additional evidence adduced by the Prosecution. Now, actions speak louder than words, but there is also other evidence that General Krstic had genocidal intent. General Krstic was standing next -- was walking next to General Mladic when they had taken Srebrenica on the 11th of July and Mladic said, "It's now time to take our revenge on the Turks." At the Hotel Fontana meetings he was sitting at the right-hand side of Mladic when Mladic threatening the Muslims with disappearance. General Krstic himself used derogatory language with respect to Muslims. On the 17th of July, he asked Captain Trivic whether he'd killed the Turks up there -- now, that intercept is taken as referring to combat, so I don't want to overstate its importance. I just merely put it forward for Your Honours' consideration about the derogatory attitude, the racist attitude that General Krstic had in relation to the Bosnian Muslims. In November 1995 -- well, the Trivic intercept, Your Honours, was Exhibit 650 and 651 at trial. In November 1995, in an interview with Drinski magazine, which was the official military magazine of the Drina Corps, he referred to Muslims as balijas, a term he himself actually recognised as a profoundly offensive for a Muslim. That's trial Exhibit 744. And Mr. Krstic -- General Krstic's testimony at 6514. That's on the trial record. Not only do you have Karadzic saying that they should all be killed, Mladic using highly threatening and derogatory language towards them, himself using racist language towards the Turks, but there is the -- the trial record shows that General Krstic's subordinates also used this type of language as they were committing their heinous crimes. The commonly-used derogatory term "Turks" and other terms were all throughout the -- the intercept material and -- and official army documents. One intercept in particular was quite striking. With respect to Muslim prisoners captured on the 13th of July, one of the speakers in this conversation refers to them as "Turk," the other one says, "Fuck them, they weren't human beings." That's trial Exhibit 513. And as I said before, the terms "Turks" and "balijas" were commonly used by the executioners when they were committing their crimes. I would like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Just if I may alert you to the fact that you have another 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Fifteen? I was going to go into the victim-impact submissions, but I -- I just will make two points in relation to that. The evidence at trial was that the surviving Bosnian Muslim population had a decreasing birthrate. That's trial transcript 5784 and 5786. That's all I'll say there, because obviously it relates to the issue of biological reproduction, and it's been an issue that's been arising in these proceedings. In conclusion, Your Honours, in respect of General Krstic's genocidal intent, it's the Prosecution's submission that on the evidence that it's put forward and on the evidence -- the additional evidence and the trial record Krstic was indispensable to the murder operation and he chose to perpetuate it. The references are, "The Main Staff was an organisational cell without manpower except the two units." That's Trial Chamber paragraph 101. I finally found it.
