It couldn't have carried out the mass crime on its own. The Drina Corps was indispensable to its commission. That's Trial Chamber judgement paragraph 266. They had to use the Drina Corps in whose area of responsibility were -- in whose area of responsibility the crimes were committed. They did it through General Krstic. He monitored and supervised it and he participated in facilitating the plan. We also say that he was in on it from the beginning and therefore all his acts in relation to the transportation of the Muslim population was also an act pursuant to the genocidal JCE. Krstic was in command and therefore control of the Drina Corps from the evening of the 13th of July, when the vast majority of prisoners were alive. He was asked to help on the 15th of July. Even at that late stage, he could have saved thousands of lives by ordering his troops not to participate and even stop the executions. Instead, he agreed to help. Thereafter the Drina Corps forces were used extensively to continue the killing operation with his knowledge. Your Honour, that concludes my submissions on the factual basis of genocidal intent. And as I only have probably about 12 minutes left now, I would just like to rely on the previous submissions I've made in respect of the MUP and the fact that the Trial Chamber found that the -- the MUP and -- and the Drina Corps, with General Krstic as their commander, were acting hand in glove together. In relation to the allegation that the MUP did the executions, the only evidence that we have that the MUP was doing executions is the additional evidence that indicates Borovcanin's groups were involved in Kravica warehouse. If you look through the trial record, there's no finding in relation to the MUP in relation to the other executions. I'm not saying that they did not participate. I'm simply saying that there's nothing to support that on the -- on the trial record. And I understand investigations are ongoing, but their submission is simply not supported in fact. I'm just going to move quickly to the Branjevo Farm issue. As I said previously, the 16th of July intercept referred to by Mr. Petrusic was actually used for two propositions: The first proposition was that General Krstic -- sorry, Colonel Popovic was reporting to General Krstic. I would refer Your Honours to the additional evidence of both Butler and Obrenovic on this. They agree that particular references in this intercept -- that the particular references in this intercept that were used by the Trial Chamber to support their conclusion remain unaffected. In fact, the additional evidence entrenches that interpretation. In relation to whether or not Bratunac Brigade -- the intercept could be used for the proposition that the Bratunac Brigade actually arrived pursuant to General Krstic's commitment to provide troops, the Prosecution puts the following proposition now: On the basis of what both Butler and Obrenovic say, it seems as though there may be another reasonable interpretation to that particular intercept; i.e., the reference to troops arriving late in that intercept might indeed be in relation to reinforcements arriving in the Zvornik Brigade area of responsibility. In short, it's the Prosecution's submission that this was not the primary piece of evidence used by the Trial Chamber to find that Bratunac Brigade personnel participated. In fact, what the Trial Chamber did is they relied on the evidence of Drazen Erdemovic. He said that soldiers arrived from Bratunac. They were wearing VRS uniforms. Now, whether or not these soldiers were members of the Bratunac Brigade is not, in the Prosecution's submission, critical. The Prosecution submits that if you just take General -- sorry, Erdemovic's evidence on its face value without making any interpretation as to whether they were actually Bratunac personnel or not, just saying that they are soldiers from Bratunac, it's our submission that those soldiers nonetheless arrived as a result of that telephone conversation. Now, there are a number of things on the record that support it. Of course, it's -- it's related to the submissions I've made previously, but basically Erdemovic testified that the men who arrived were soldiers from Bratunac who were wearing VRS uniforms. Therefore, it can be safely assumed that they were not paramilitaries or mercenaries; they were regular soldiers. In the intercept, Beara confirms that is the MUP won't help, so we know that these those people are not the MUP. The Main Staff had two assets, the 10th Division and the 65th Protection Regiment. The 10th Division was already there. That's the unit that Erdemovic was a member of and was committing the murders. There's no suggestion on the record in any of the evidence that it was the 65th Protection Regiment. Further, if it was the 65th Protection Regiment, Beara wouldn't have to ask Krstic for help because the 65th Protection Regiment is not a subordinate unit of Krstic; it is a subordinate unit of the Main Staff. In conclusion, Your Honours, these executioners didn't arrive at a specified execution point in a remote region in a Zvornik Brigade area of responsibility in order to commit murders by accident or coincidence. They were VRS soldiers and they were sent there. The evidence on the record says that General Krstic, in response to General Beara's -- Colonel Beara's request offered to help. The only conclusion that one can reach is that the soldiers referred to by Erdemovic are in fact the soldiers that were sent by General Krstic and therefore the extra added element of participation in respect of this intercept remains; that is, the substance of the Trial Chamber's verdict -- or finding in relation to the 15 July intercept and the delivery of personnel is not effected. That concludes my submissions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. Our scheduling now would be somewhat affected by how my colleagues feel about asking questions now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Well, if we are going to have questions, it would only be fair that we have a break now for the interpreters, and that would leave us the necessary leeway. So we will now rise for 30 minutes and then resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. Before turning to the reply by the Defence, I will invite my colleagues, the learned Judges, to ask questions. Judge Pocar, the vice-president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, President. I wish to thank the Prosecution for its contribution to clarifying the issues -- some issues of this appeal, as I'm grateful to the Defence for their contribution this morning. From the Prosecution, I would like now to have some clarification in order to be sure as to what the Prosecution position is on a couple of points concerning the notion of genocide they maintain. Mr. Farrell, I take it that it is your position that for the purposes of Article 4 of the ICTY Statute, or indeed Article 2 of the Genocide Convention, a part of a group or a substantial part of a group should be considered independently, irrespective of the whole of the group, without entering into consideration of proportions of that -- of the size of that part, vis-a-vis the entire group; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: If it is so, does this entail that it is also your position that for the purposes of this appeal it would be irrelevant to regard as a targeted group the Muslim population of Srebrenica or the Muslim population of Bosnia as a whole, provided the number of people killed is such that per se may be considered as representing a substantial part of the Muslim population in the region?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: If that is so, have I -- and this is the question I wanted to put to you: Have I to assume that your position is the killing of 7500 men of military age or the attempt of killing 15.000, as you mentioned, constitutes genocide because it -- that killing by itself -- represents a substantial part of the Muslim population, or is it your position that that killing constitutes genocide because it has or had the effect of causing the physical disappearance of the entire group represented by the Muslim community of Srebrenica? I have the impression that you pleaded both positions, but I may be wrong. And therefore I ask for clarification. Do you maintain both of these positions or just one of them? And if you maintain both, wouldn't you see there some contradiction as to the definition of the part of a group in the context of the notion of genocide or are you pleading both of them as alternative positions, since both may support the Prosecution's case? Which is exactly your clarification on that point? I would be grateful for the clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Pocar. As you're correct, both positions were actually put if forward. The attempt I tried to make was that the Prosecution position is that the judgement stands for the proposition that the killing of the men leads to the destruction or annihilation, as they say, of the Bosnian Muslims at Srebrenica. The Defence took the position that the Trial Chamber's judgement only stood for the proposition that the intent was to destroy the men and the men only and that that part was numerically too small. Therefore, the Prosecution's position is that the Trial Chamber was correct that the targeting of the men resulted in the destruction of the group in Srebrenica and that group is a substantial part. If the -- if the Prosecution's reading of that judgement is incorrect, it's still the Prosecution's position, in the alternative, that the intention to kill somewhere between 10 and 15 thousand men on the basis of their group characteristics would be sufficient for the in-part requirement of genocide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. That's very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Judge Schomburg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Coming back just to the figures you mentioned, 7.500, 15.000. Are these figures, in your view, really of importance? Isn't it true from your point of view that genocide is a very specific crime, that -- and not as usual we start analysing the acts and conducts and then inferring the intent? That's relatively easy. But as to the fact that there is a surplus of specific intent necessary for committing this crime, it's extremely difficult to identify what is this specific intent. Would you share with me the view that in case a person had the specific intent and only one person was killed, that this can amount to genocide?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be correct that even if nobody would have been killed, that under the Statute foreseen only for the crime of genocide the punishability of the attempt, this would amount to the attempt of genocide?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So having listened carefully to the arguments -- the factual arguments of both parties, it's really difficult. The arguments of the one side seem to be -- the factual arguments seem to be compelling from your side; then listening to your contribution, one really seems to be convinced it can be the only one solution. Therefore, we have to be extremely careful in analysing the facts and, as you correctly said, the acts and the conduct of Mr. Krstic. You drew our attention to a number of documents: For example, the famous Annex 7 of the 13th of July, 1995, which indeed shows that this document was signed - apparently the authenticity is not contested - by Major General Radislav Krstic the 13th of July. But here it reads: "The Main Corps forces will continue to defend the chief lines." And after, two lines or three lines later: "The purpose is to disarm these first Muslim forces, protect the population and property, and at the same time secure the lines of defence from attacks from behind." So a number of documents seem to be in part ambiguous; some convincing in one direction, some in the other direction. Why do I come back to this? Because I think a careful analysis is needed to make a distinction between the intent to kill, the intent to exterminate, and the intent to commit genocide, in the words of Honourable Judge Wald, the crime of crimes. Therefore -- unfortunately, I haven't got yet an answer from the side of the Prosecution. Given the case, there was on a higher level this specific intent. And bringing all the factual evidence together, in your submission, what would be the final result as to the fact that we have under Article 4 to determine what of the following acts Article 4(3) are punishable in this case, genocide or complicity in genocide? And it was not without reason - and I am convinced that a number of people in this Tribunal -- in this courtroom were surprised when I asked a line of questions -- put a line of questions to Witness Deronjic relating already to 1991 December and the beginning of 1992. Maybe you have asked what has all this to do with this. I think, couldn't it be true that as to the fact that the Prosecution is limiting its case to Srebrenica and not trying to show and give us an overall view, starting, I believe - I don't know, but to a certain extent one can rely as there was a guilty plea on this - starting already by instructions given in 1991, that one can come to the conclusion that at least on a higher level there was such an intent? Could I please hear your submissions on this in case one comes to the conclusion that on a higher level there was in fact -- and, of course, based on the evidence before us -- that there was this specific intent, at least on a higher level. What would be then the role of the accused in our case?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you. You've raised some factual issues, which I'll presume for the sake of your argument, of course, and some legal issues. Without -- I have a number of responses, but without sounding overly simplistic, if the finding that this convicted appellant has -- has the genocidal intent, as found by the Trial Chamber, then of course that -- if there are others who were higher up in the chain of command that have the similar intent or are part of the JCE, then it makes no difference, obviously. He's still a member and will be final liable based on the Trial Chamber's conclusion. The next question that appears -- or at least I'll assume is included is if there is a distinction in your mind, either in terms of fact or -- fact, meaning the acts, or knowledge between those who might be higher up and -- and someone in the position of a mid-level or a lower level, hypothetically. Then the question becomes: What are the elements, the required elements, for those? Complicity, aiding and abetting, and genocide, I think, is essentially what it comes down to. If the person in the hypothetical case - we're talking about in this case, where it's a General, Main Staff level or General Krstic level, and if they are in the JCE, then it's not a problem, because they'll have to have the mens rea. In the Prosecution's submission, first of all -- this is before Your Honours in the Ntakirutimana appeal, so I won't prejudice the end result in that case as we've appealed the modes of liability in the crime. In my submission, the starting point is that complicity, at least as I understand it and the way that the Prosecution has argued it recently, it's not a crime. It's a mode of liability. Complicity is the manner in which you commit the crime. It's the same as aiding and abetting. Though in Article 4 of the Statute complicity is listed as one of the acts that is punishable with other forms of inchoate crimes and incitement and other forms. It's not -- in my respectful submission, it's actually not a separate crime, it's a form of participation in addition to aiding and abetting. The Semanza Trial Chamber judgement in the ICTR has held that because of the drafting and the incorporation of the Genocide Convention directly into our Statute -- in this case the Rwanda Statute, of course -- combined with 6(1) has created an overlap in the form of liability, and that form of liability is in Article 7(1), aiding and abetting, and in Article 4, complicity. The only distinction that I can conceive of between complicity and aiding and abetting is there was some reference in the ICTR jurisprudence that complicity actually would include accessory after the fact. The aiding and abetting, as defined by our jurisprudence in Tadic, would include assisting, encouraging, or lending moral support. For the most part, unless you could incorporate some type of accessory or assistance of the fact into complicity, which is not found in aiding and abetting, then for all intents and purposes they are the same. The mode of participation is one of someone who as an accomplice commits the acts. The distinction then between aiding and abetting and complicity, if I can place them together for the sake of my response, and the committing of genocide would be that the acts would be one of assistance for complicity or aiding and abetting, while for genocide it would be the actual commission or the direct acts. The next question is: If that's the difference between the act element, is there a difference between the mental element? And it's the Prosecution's position that there is. I appreciate that there is some jurisprudence in the ICTR that says that complicity requires a specific intent and aiding and abetting requires knowledge. With respect, that doesn't make -- that doesn't make -- well, in the Prosecution's submission, it's a bit illogical. In fact, depending on the -- some say it's the other way around, and some indicate that you need aiding and abetting. The difference between aiding and abetting is a particular manner of participation but you would still need the specific intent. The Prosecution's position in Ntakirutimana, which is before the Appeals Chamber, is that complicity and aiding and abetting require knowledge. The form -- the direct form of participation, the commission for genocide, requires the specific intent. And that the Prosecution will be arguing in that case that complicity as a mode of participation and aiding and abetting as a mode of participation are for those persons who aid and abet to assist with the knowledge of the crime to be committed and take steps to assist the perpetrator with that full knowledge. This Tribunal has, as you're fully aware, Your Honour, has decided in Tadic that aiding and abetting requires knowledge. This Tribunal has also held in the Krnojelac Appeals Chamber judgement that aiding and abetting a specific intent crime requires knowledge. The next step is whether or not aiding and abetting the specific intent crime of genocide requires knowledge. The only distinction that I can think of is the actual wording of Article 4(2) of the Statute, which specifically says that "Genocide means any of the following acts committed with intent to destroy." Now, that could be interpreted as being that the acts -- the acts must be committed with an intent to destroy. It would be my submission though -- this is obviously without any chance to brief this issue and obviously we've got submissions in the Ntakirutimana which I don't want to prejudice - but it would by my submission that that's for the commission of genocide. That's not for acts of complicity or aiding and abetting. You must have someone who committed genocide by the act element with the specific intent. That's the requirement. The complicity is not necessary to have the specific intent and the specific -- the case law, Krnojelac and others that deal with aiding and abetting, in my respectful submission, for specific intent crimes would be the same, which is knowledge. I don't know if that provides any assistance, but that's the general position of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this. Just for the purpose of clarification, because, as you no doubt know, in Akayesu they found a solution just the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I want to refrain from any comments relating to this. However, your submission comes down to the point saying that complicity in genocide is more or less lex specialis to aiding and abetting in genocide because you need the same mens rea and all the other elements we know from other cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I would have to give it further thought, but I think that would be the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Maybe this is the reason why you did not plea aiding and abetting in this case but complicity in genocide.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: There is, I think, to be frank -- there has been in the past with the previous indictment some uncertainty of the relationship of the three elements - genocide, complicity, and aiding and abetting - which you've obviously identified. And the practice in the ICTR had been to charge complicity as a crime, and that practice has actually resulted in one case for a conviction for complicity, which may appear problematic, as it's a mode of liability, at least in the Prosecution's submission in Ntakirutimana, but there are -- there is some support for pleading it as a crime. As a result, if complicity, which you've already identified -- if complicity has the same elements of aiding and abetting, then it just simply just stands in the place of or in the shoes of aiding and abetting. But in the Prosecution's submission, the difficulty actually comes when you find the elements if you accept they're the same and you find the elements of knowledge and the element of the acts necessary for assisting, lending encouragement, and you have 7(1), aiding and abetting the crime, and you have the charge of complicity of the crime. That's where the difficulty comes, I think, because in the Prosecution's submission, they're the same. Semanza attempted to deal with that by looking at the specific count and finding out which count was more specific to the findings and then accepting that count and not finding on the other one. If that's -- if that's not too convoluted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: If Judge Schomburg has finished, I will call on Judge Shahabuddeen, who has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] .

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Farrell, I just want to make sure that I have the same appreciation of the legal character of the case you're putting forward as you do. Now, it is written that an accused person has to be personally, criminally culpable. That is a basis of criminal responsibility. But that does not conflict with a certain duality in approach. I would classify this as a direct and indirect approach. You may have a direct approach, in which the Prosecution sets out to prove that the accused has individually intended a certain result and that he individually participated in the actus reus leading to that result. I have in mind this is one branch of your case, much stressed by your learned colleague. I have in mind that there is another branch of your case which is connected with the concept of joint criminal enterprise, to which you and Mr. Sepenuk referred. This is what I would call -- do forgive me. I am coining my own language here -- the indirect mode. I have the impression that one part of your case is saying that there was a common-purpose enterprise, that the accused was a party to this common-purpose enterprise. And pursuant to this common purpose, a certain criminal result ensued. Therefore, he is liable without more -- "without more," I mean this: You don't have to prove that individually he had any particular intent or that individually he participated in the actus reus. All you have to prove is that there was a common-purpose enterprise, he was a party to this common purpose, and that a certain criminal result ensued. Is -- does the second part of that analysis apply to your case, or does it not? Have I misunderstood?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: No, not at all, Your Honour. Maybe I won't say it in the best of words, as I probably don't know the case as well as my colleague. But the acts - and I'm sure you're fully aware of this, Your Honour - but the acts that are done individually in this case, there are some acts that are done individually. The specific provision of men to assist in executions, of course, would be in and of itself a act under 7(1) and could be a form of liability. But the -- and then, of course, as you're fully aware, the -- this is the Prosecution's submission that the acts in total are acts of someone who is involved in and facilitating a joint criminal enterprise. All of them, his individual acts, are his role he plays and the contribution he makes. So I'm not exactly sure that I'm characterising correctly, but I would say that it's not simply that he -- he's got two roles. He does play a role; he plays a role that is a -- provides, and is of course indispensable, but for joint criminal enterprise he participates and provides substantial contribution. And he shares the purpose in this case, and was required to by the -- by the law under the JCE. So I -- I think it would be more accurate though - maybe the facts don't reflect it as well as the theory would - but that his acts, his individual acts, as the commander of the Drina Corps, those -- those acts constitute the role that he plays in the joint criminal enterprise and that those acts are his substantial contribution, because within the enterprise he has a role to play and so do others, and there's certain tasks are assigned to them in that sense in that they have certain functions, and without them the criminal enterprise would like differently. I guess in a simplistic way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, thank you. May I give you a case --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: -- which you can look up. I was look at it last night, and your colleague across the way might look at it also. It's the case of McKinnon against Her Majesty's advocate, a Scottish case, 2003 -- 2003 SLT, decided on the 13th of February this year by a five-member Bench of the High Court of Justiciary in Scotland. It seemed to say that where you are relying on common purpose then it is only necessary to prove that the accused was a party to the common enterprise and that a certain criminal result followed without any necessity to prove that he himself had individually any criminal intent or that he himself had individually participated in the actus reus. It's an interesting case. Both sides might like to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I look forward to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. I -- I have a follow-up question to questions asked by my distinguished colleague Judge Schomburg. His questions and your answers helped throw some light on the question of standard of knowledge or mens rea required for aiding and abetting the crime of genocide and complicity in the crime of genocide. My question would touch on the additional prong: How would you define the standard of knowledge which would be required for 7(3) responsibility, namely command responsibility, in the case of genocide? We do know that command responsibility requires a standard -- normally a standard of knowledge which does not rise to special intent. We know the special problems of special intent in the context of genocide.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: The -- I haven't given it much thought, to be honest, Mr. President, but I think that the standard would remain the should have known standard and the reason is not because -- his acts are acts of failing to take steps or failing to punish. He's not being -- he's not being convicted for his direct commission but for failing to fulfil his obligations under international humanitarian law. It would seem a little bit incongruous that a commander whose subordinates are causing less serious crimes should have an obligation to prevent them once he finds out. But a commander whose subordinates are committing genocide should have no obligation to prevent them if he doesn't share the intent or at least, he has no obligation to prevent them in the sense that he won't be criminally liable as a result before an international Tribunal. That to me would be, well, illogical. But I'm sorry, that's as far as I can assist you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. If there are no other questions from the Bench, we will now turn to the reply by the Defence, which has 30 minutes for it. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My colleague, Mr. Petrusic, will speak first, and with Your Honours' permission, I will speak second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in view of the time, as we are approaching the end of the working day - and I assume that our interpreters are already tired - I shall comment very briefly on some of the parts of the submissions made by the Prosecution. Namely, the Prosecution would wish to establish a link between the then-president, Karadzic, General Mladic, and the appointment of General Krstic to the position of corps commander. All are relying on the testimony of Mr. Deronjic. There is no dispute that Mr. Deronjic in his testimony said that he made a request to President Karadzic that the until-then commander, General Zivanovic, should be replaced. And this happened sometime in May 1995. However, it is a fact that Mr. Deronjic in his testimony never said that he had personally suggested to President Karadzic that the replacement should be General Krstic. So it would be wrong to infer, as the Prosecution does, that General Krstic was in a sense Karadzic's man or a man that the then-president, Karadzic, had confidence in. Furthermore, there was reference to intercepts and the role of Lieutenant Colonel Popovic. But in the trial itself and in the critical period when the crimes were being committed, there is not a single piece of evidence or intercept that proves a direct communication between General Krstic and Lieutenant Colonel Popovic. For the sake of truth, it should be noted that on two occasions, in the notebooks of the operators who were intercepting these conversations, there is an indication that a message was left to the effect that Popovic had asked for the General. In one place it says "General Krstic," but we also don't have the return evidence that the link between them was established or that that message was passed on to General Krstic. My learned friend from the Prosecution says that as a member of the joint criminal enterprise and engaging in the organisation of the bussing and the buses that were taking the Muslims towards Tisca, that those unloaded, 28 of them, were later executed. I wish to remind this Honourable Chamber that it was this location, the Tisca location, that General Krstic issued orders to his subordinate units of the 12th of July at 13.05 as to how they should treat civilians who were passing through going to Muslim-controlled territory. Obviously somebody did not respect his order. Finally, when the Prosecution was talking about -- about the role of Vinko Pandurevic and his return to the zone of the Zvornik Brigade, to the location where massive crimes were committed, Dragan Obrenovic in his testimony says the following: "I assumed that he - Major Jevdjevic - could link me with General Krstic, and that is what I did. I spoke briefly first to Jevdjevic and asked him that I would like to get in touch with General Krstic. And of course the line was not even interrupted. Shortly after that, I reached General Krstic on the line. I told him briefly that the situation was critical, that Zvornik would simply fall, and that more than half of Zvornik would be destroyed. He asked me why I was so scared. He obviously did not understand and did not comprehend what was going on." Your Honours, that would end my submissions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I will now turn to Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May it please the Judges of this Honourable Chamber. I have just a few points to make. I -- first of all, I think I gave too glib and facile an answer, Judge Meron, to your question before about what if all the women had been killed. And the reason that occurred to me is Mr. Farrell's comment about how there seems to be an apparent inconsistency with what I said, based on what Mr. Schabas said in part about killing the women and the b boys vis-a-vis killing the men. And I thought your question was more the part of a part again. It just occurred to me that, you know, the women constitute a part of a part, and for the same reason that we advance with respect to the men, i.e. a lack of substantial and no interpret to kill the Bosnian Muslim group as such, I said it would make no difference. But under another thesis, i.e., that the Bosnian Muslim group of Srebrenica is what we're talking about, certainly it could make and would make a difference. Because when the -- when the women were displaced, all of the women with the elderly men and the younger men, there certainly was still an opportunity, despite the low birthrate, as the Prosecution mentioned -- there's still the opportunity for that group -- for that group of Bosnian Muslims to survive. If the women were killed, that would not be the case. Certainly, eventually, biologically the group would die out. Now, that's aside from questions about whether you could consider other people coming in and that kind of thing. But we don't have that situation. I'm very pleased we don't have that situation. I hope we never have that situation. But I wanted to clarify that, Your Honour. The second thing is Branjevo Farm. One of the privileges I've had in this case is working against a very highly professional Prosecutor's Office, and the one disappointment I have -- and I do not mean this personally -- but the one disappointment I have is the Prosecution's position on the Branjevo Farm executions. To the Defence, it's crystal clear that the Prosecution has come nowhere near proving beyond a reasonable doubt that General Krstic ordered these executions, ordered men from the Bratunac Brigade to assist in Branjevo Farm and/or Pilica Dom executions. And by the way, I think the briefs -- our briefs are pretty clear on this. And obviously, Your Honours, anything I don't say now or anything I haven't said, please, we submit our briefs. We rely on what's in our briefs. The briefs alone, I think, made our point. But now with the additional testimony of -- of Obrenovic and the addition until testimony of Butler, I would say -- and again, I hate to be absolutist about anything in this morass of the law, but my goodness, there's a total failure of proof on that point by the Prosecution. What they've done is they've taken this language, "I'll see what I can do" and rather than interpret it in the light most favourable to General Krstic, rather than interpret it in the light of the principle of in dubio pro re, they say, "No, no, this is the opening salvo." They've parlayed that into the beginning of a -- almost a plan by General Krstic, certainly a course of conduct, to send men, men from the Bratunac Brigade, to -- to assist in the executions. And all they have on this -- all this have is this equivocal comment "I'll see what I can do." So us he's simply using an American expression trying to get Colonel Beara off his back: "I'll see what I can do. I'll see what I can do. I'll see what I can do." The fact is he did nothing. The only evidence they have is they have these five men in VRS uniforms. But the fact is, as Erdemovic testified, and Mr. Butler testified, and we've set forth in our brief, one of these men was from the Panteri unit of the Eastern Bosnia Corps, not from the Drina Corps at all. And again, the men who arrived from the Bratunac Brigade - it's now absolutely clear - arrived late but they arrive late to assist in the battle, not to assist in executions. The government -- Prosecution should confess error on that point, just like we conceded forcible transfer. Just like we conceded forcible transfer, they should confess error on this point, because they have no case on the Branjevo Farm executions. The -- on behalf of -- I know I speak on behalf of Mr. Petrusic when I say that it has been a privilege for us to appear before this Court on such an important case. And the only thing that's truly crucial here is to get it right. We came very close to not getting it right when we filed our initial briefs. Again, there were time constraints, time limitations, and it's only as the months have gone on and that Mr. Petrusic and I, trying to immerse ourselves in this situation - and by the way, Your Honours don't need me to tell you that, you know, one of the Prosecutors here was a trial Prosecutor. Mr. Harmon, Mr. Cayley, Mr. McCloskey, a very formidable and experienced team, and any set of Defence lawyers could come in - in this case, it happened to be two Serbian Defence lawyers, Mr. Petrusic, Mr. Tomislav Visnjic, good lawyers and fine gentlemen. But talk about equality of arms. There is a catching-up process, and I take my hat off to Mr. Farrell. Mr. Farrell's knowledge is certain aspects of the law is encyclopaedic. And I couldn't even begin -- I mean that sincerely, Your Honour. And I couldn't even begin to try to match him on that kind of thing. But the important thing is to get it right, and thank goodness we finally saw the whole Commission of Experts point. And what I wanted to say is one of the reasons it's been a privilege to appear before this Tribunal is that I don't know we could have done this, certainly, I only know an American courtroom. This is my first experience here. In an American court you submit briefs ask then you have an half hour aside for an oral argument -- in a Supreme Court I believe it's an hour. And sometimes the Prosecution or Defence will get a minute or two of words out and then there's this immediate, I'll call it, confrontation by the Court. So what a pleasure it has been - and we thank you so much to allow us -- to have allowed us to make our full argument in this case, because it's very important in this case - your Honours don't need me to tell you this - not only for General Krstic but for the victims at Srebrenica, for world history, to get it right in this case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before turning to the last item on our agenda, an important item, a personal address by General Krstic, let me tell you on behalf of the entire Bench that we are here to do justice and that both the Prosecution and the Defence have greatly assisted the Bench in their very professional arguments. This is a very difficult case. This is a case of historic importance, and it is therefore so important that we have had very professional assistance from both sides, the Defence and the Prosecution. And now, the last item on our agenda is: Should General -- General Krstic, would you rise. If you -- should you wish so, would you like to address the Court briefly, General?

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I am addressing you not availing myself of the right that I am accorded to but the respect you have shown me by the very fact of giving me the floor. My Defence team has presented a great many things thus far and has done its best for me, and that is why I am not going to speak of any facts or address any legal issues. Srebrenica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I think so you might be going a bit too fast for the interpreters. Just a little bit slower, General.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Srebrenica, in July 1995, to all the participants in it, brought evil. To the Muslims of that Eastern Bosnian small town, the victims, they had pain and suffering; and to the Serbs it brought great shame because somebody dared to blemish the lofty traditions of Serb officers dating back to the start of the twentieth century and even before that. They were trampled upon. And this illustrious tradition affected me personally. It is why I chose to become an officer in the first place. The Serbs, unfortunately, throughout their past but not through any will of their own had to wage many wars, and I'm only going to mention those dating back to the beginning of the twentieth century and also the middle of the twentieth century -- 1912, 1913, 1914, and 1941 -- but never - and when I say "never," I mean truly never - did they commit any evil crimes. Their traditions of warfare are illustrious, right up until that July of 1995, and even then right until the entry of the Serb forces in Srebrenica that was true. I who myself led the operation, as well as my subordinates, up until then never violated any of the rules of war nor the provisions and laws of the Geneva Conventions. And then instead of going to military victory, because the 28th Division was a legitimate military target, we had this terrible shame fall upon us because the intelligent and wise kept silent and the others spoke up. Someone said that "When you have a war, it is always the wise who remain silent and the fools who speak out, and they shout it out." They were loud and clear. Ask we had to keep silent. Never before or after that did I or my subordinate commanders hear their speech, but we learnt about what they did. We learnt of their evil acts, which we were not able to put right. Your Honours, God will punish me if I have done wrong. You will make your ruling and decision in conformity with the law and in keeping with your consciences. But I would like to prevail upon you and tell you that on that day, the 12th of July, 1995, in the early afternoon hours, with my army, with my men, I had left the area and went in quite another direction to quite another front. Those others spoke the language of evil then, and neither I myself or my subordinates ever joined them. Your Honours, I cannot but -- remain silent and not tell you this: I would like to say that I deeply regret all the victims and I share the pain and suffering that their families have had to experience, and my condolences do not date just from this day but they were always present with me from the very first moment that I learnt of what had happened. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, General Krstic. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Our hearings of this appeal have now come to an end, and I thank you again and we will now rise.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.14 p.m.
